speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, namely, the fact that many fertilizer dealers in Manitoba are out of fertilizer, or very nearly so, because of the almost total lack of railway cars to carry this product from its source to the dealer. If this situation continues, it could spell disaster not only for the dealers but for their farmer customers. The supply of fertilizer in Manitoba for the critical spring period can only be described as desperate. Accordingly, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart):
That the Minister of Transport use all the power and persuasion he can muster to ensure that by this weekend a sufficient number of railway cars will be directed to the hauling of fertilizer, and that these cars will continue hauling fertilizer for the balance of the spring seeding period.

Mr. Speaker, some days ago I received recommendations from the three hon. members of my party representing the London district and I have started to look into the matter. I have asked my officials to review it and to see if we can find an accommodation. As soon as I can reach a solution within the law, I shall be delighted to announce it. 1 am not sure if it is possible, but I shall do my best.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Monday I believe, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) raised a question of privilege regarding the CBC coverage of the Social Credit Party convention. I contacted the CBC to get a reply to the question that was asked and this is what I was told.
Last August, the CBC informed the various parties that it had modified its policy of automatic and live coverage of leadership conventions, and that in future it would consider several factors in its editorial decisions for such coverage. There are now several factors to be considered, for example the position that the party occupies nationally, the importance of the convention, the political interest that it provokes throughout the country, the impact of the candidates and of the orientation of their platform, as they appeared throughout the leadership race.
The Social Credit Party convention was to be held in June, possibly in the midst of an election. It was pushed ahead to the beginning of May and was therefore rushed. Candidacies were uncertain until the convention was held. The participation of some important candidates was even doubtful. None of the leadership candidates made a Canada-wide tour. The official nomination of some candidates was apparently made only at the convention.
The French services division of the CBC reported the leadership convention in its radio and television news broadcasts, and decided to review the convention in a one hour peak time program on Sunday night, both on radio and on television. The English television network of the CBC decided to broadcast a half hour special on the convention Sunday night. Monday night, Newsmagazine did an interview with the new leader and Mr. Gilles Caouette. Over the weekend, the English radio network aired news bulletins of the convention. CBC reports were comparable to if not better than those of other networks.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise a question of privilege which has come to my notice in the last few minutes. It concerns an issue of which Your Honour and many members of the House are well aware and which we have been raising over the last few weeks, namely, the recent memo that went out from National Revenue respecting the political activities of charitable organizations. I am glad the Acting Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) is here, because I think this concerns the rights and privileges of all members of parliament.
Hon. members will recall that a couple of years ago when a similar issue was raised, the then minister, now Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), was in charge of the department and I asked him at that time whether or not it would be possible to have a complete list of the charitable organizations which were registered as having a special tax status with National Revenue. The minister and his officials made it clear that, while they could not provide the list, there was public access to the list and that an official from my office could go to the department and have a look at the list to see who was registered as having that special tax status.
A few minutes ago I was informed that a representative of my office was informed by the assistant deputy minister of Revenue Canada in charge of legislation that this policy has been changed this year and that they will no longer allow public access to their list of charitable organizations. Apparently their reason is that the list contains confidential information. Even apart from that, the official refused to provide such a list with the confidential information taken out, with the simple comment that it was an unreasonable request.
I find it passing strange, in the light of the fact that there has been great anxiety already generated among the community of more than 36,000 organizations in this country about what is the intent of the government with respect to the memorandum which was circulated, and in light of the fact that every charitable organization, to my knowledge, when it raises money indicates in a public way that it has this tax status. I can only believe that this secrecy is not for the protection of the organizations but in some way for the protection of government officials. I suspect that is the reason why the department has changed the position which existed until this year of allowing public access to the list of those who are registered as having a special tax status with National Revenue. I know it is perhaps not possible for the acting minister today to take action to reverse this very serious decision, but I certainly hope the situation will be cleared up shortly because it affects my rights and privileges and, I am sure, the rights and privileges of every member on both sides of the House.

MR. BRISCO-ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED DIVERSION OF KOOTENAY RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. During the question period I directed a question to the Minister of State for the Environment (Mr. Marchand). Subsequently another member of this party addressed a supplementary question to the minister, and on each occasion the minister indicated that his pronouncements during the question period, when we are seeking the official position of the government, represent his personal view only which he held before he became a member of the cabinet and which he still holds as a member of the cabinet.
My question of privilege pertains to the fact that the public pronouncements which the minister made to the press, both at Athalmer and to the public in the community of Creston recently, where the minister was on official government business and where he presented a cheque for $55,000 to the Creston Valley Wildlife Management Authority-something that I certainly appreciate-were made in his official capacity. He met these people in his capacity as minister and never once did he indicate to the public that his opposition to the Kootenay diversion was a personal position. The minister succeeded in getting himself boxed in very successfully by questions from our own member. At the same time, while the minister felt that that uncomfortable box was a laughing matter, I can assure him that the people of Kootenay West, and indeed the people of Okanagan-Kootenay, do not consider the Kootenay River diversion a laughing matter.
The following question arises therefore: can the minister, speaking for the government, provide an answer of the nature that the minister has provided when he stated he is giving a personal opinion and not the official government position during the official proceedings of the House, during the question period? Surely members on this side, in addressing questions to ministers are seeking the official position of the government, not the personal opinion of any minister.
If the minister is not providing his personal opinion, then who from among the ministers is responsible for providing the official government position? Certainly the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) is well aware of the fact that his pronouncements with reference to the MacGregor Diversion, when he was responsible for the Department of the
Privilege-Mr. Brisco
Environment, represented the position of the government, in terms of its opposition to the MacGregor Diversion and the reasons for it, when he spoke both in the House and in the standing committee, and I commend him for it. I respect the minister for putting forward the government's view opposing the diversion. That was the position of both the minister and the department, it was the official position of the government. What we heard today, in response to my question to the minister of State, was not an official pronouncement, unless the minister is prepared to rise in his place and confirm that indeed he made an official pronouncement.
I wonder in what position this puts me, the people in Kootenay West, and members of the House who may subsequently wish to put questions to ministers and who become recipients of personal viewpoints rather than the official position of the government.
Hon Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport): Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. In the absence of the Minister of State for the Environment (Mr. Marchand), I should like to make a few brief comments. First of all, I think it was rather unwise of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) to suggest that the Minister of State treated the issue as a laughing matter. I think the hon. member, as well as many other members of the House, know that the laughter which occurred was a result of a fairly amusing remark made by one of his Conservative colleagues in the House, and not in relation to the issue at all. But whether or not he knew that, the hon. member for Kootenay West knew that the Minister of State for the Environment does not treat any of these issues as a laughing matter.
Obviously it is possible for a minister to have personal opinions and to have expressed them before he became a member of the cabinet, and then to be in the interesting position of having to discuss that fact. Whether or not the minister referred to his statements as personal statements when he was out in the Kootenays may be a question open to further determination. Very often a minister does say that this is a personal opinion, and it is not carried by the press at all. In any case, obviously a minister may express personal opinions and need not always describe them as such, but has to live with whether or not they accord with government policy or decisions made later on.
In this case government decisions will be taken from time to time as the issue arises, in the case of transport, as questions relating to navigable waters are determined, in the question of the environment, after the appropriate analysis and studies have taken place, and then a governmental decision is taken. I do not think that is impeded in any way by the expression of a personal opinion by either a minister or a backbencher on any side of the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lloyd R. Crouse (South Shore) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
That this House condemns the federal Minister of Fisheries for his failure to consult and co-operate with provincial fisheries ministers and fishermen prior to establishing arbitrary rules and regulations which are harmful to the fishermen, and for his failure to develop a positive policy for the protection and development of the Canadian fishing industry in order to derive maximum advantage for Canadians from the extended jurisdiction.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity on this opposition day to comment on a number of problems presently facing the fishing industry. When looking over recent events which have occurred within the industry, 1 cannot help but be concerned over the statements and the actions of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) as they relate to this important industry.
It is obvious that Liberal supporters are very much concerned during an election campaign about how fishermen may vote, and then the promises come as thick and as fast as the capelin run off the coast of Newfoundland. However, after the election is over, the promises are soon forgotten. This is
obviously Liberal policy. We should always remember that it was the present Prime Minister who called Liberal supporters "idiots" and who said that the political philosophy of the Liberal party is simplicity itself: "say anything, promise anything, think anything, but please put us into power." This scheme has worked very well for the Liberals quite a number of times.
From looking at the polls, it now appears that the electorate are unhappy over the manner in which they have been manipulated. Equally it is obvious that they plan to do something about it, if they are given an opportunity.
We in the Progressive Conservative party are not the only ones concerned over present Liberal fisheries policies. For example, at the recent Liberal policy convention held in Ottawa, between February 24 to February 26, the following resolution was adopted:
That there be co-ordinated development of the fisheries within the regions of Canada.
Even the Liberal party realizes that there is not a comprehensive and co-ordinated fisheries policy in Canada. For this reason, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment should be censured. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment appears content to rest upon the laurels of obtaining the 200-mile limit. If one were to believe the Liberal propaganda of the time, the limit should have been implemented at least five years earlier. We believe the attainment of the 200-mile limit was only the first step. Much more needs to be done for the rehabilitation of our fisheries.
At the Liberal policy convention this spring, delegates cried out for a co-ordinated fisheries policy. It is no wonder they did so, especially when one looks at the recent legislative record of the Trudeau government. During the past two sessions of parliament only two bills were introduced and passed pertaining to fisheries. However, one of these, the small craft harbours bill, allows the minister to set unrestricted licence fees for the use of these harbours. My colleagues and I requested that the minister bear in mind the high unemployment and low income levels of Atlantic Canada and to defer any introduction of licence fees for at least five years. However, this reasonable request was howled down and voted down by the Liberal party.
When speaking of the Trudeau legislative record, it is worth noting that we are still waiting for the promised legislation which will create a separate department of fisheries. In February the Liberal policy convention felt that a separate department was imminent. One resolution which passed read as follows:
We applaud the decision of the government to create by an act of parliament a separate department of Fisheries, and recommend that the new department have a strong mandate in the management of the Fisheries and oceans, with the resources and manpower it requires.
The latter sentence is a point which we have been advocating in this House for years. It is little wonder that many commentators describe the Liberal policy resolutions as being nothing more than direct steals from Conservative policies. As

May 11, 1978

I said before, we are still waiting for this legislation from Pierre the procrastinator. Interestingly enough it was the Trudeau government which in 1970 needlessly ended the existence of the separate Department of Fisheries. And then what happened? During the 1974 election the Prime Minister-I think at that time he was in Digby, Nova Scotia-when he found that the heat was on one of his candidates promised at the time that he would recreate a separate department. Does this sound familiar? Of course after the election the promises were forgotten. That election was 1974, and this is 1978, and still today we are asking, "why has this not been done in this House four years later?"
The promises of this government for a separate department are nothing more than empty promises. An effective fisheries policy requires successful management, and quotas form the basis for the successful management of the 200-mile limit. However, sound quotas rely upon good research. For example, we believe the minister and his scientists overlooked an important fact when establishing the 1977 quotas for capelin and squid.
Fishermen complain about the excessive catches of these species, because they believe they provide the food for the other groundfish in the sea. Of course they do provide food for the cod, which is one of the main fisheries resources that must be restored. Cod in the fishing industry is king, and every effort must be made to restore this particular species. In 1976 the quotas on capelin and squid were 480,000 tons and 99,000 tons respectively. In 1977 they were increased to 500,000 tons and 104,000 tons respectively.
By permitting excessive catches of capelin and squid by foreign fleets, the minister is contributing to the continued decline of our over-all fishing stock because many of our important fish stocks will eat their own if capelin and squid are not available. Yet, only a week or two ago in committee when we raised the question about quotas on squid and their availability, the scientists and representatives from the minister's department said that they do not know if squid live longer than a year and a half, or two years. They admitted in committee that they really know very little about the life cycles of these two important fish species that feed the other fish.
More scientific research is necessary. We need to know what kind of changes in abundance and distribution occur as a result of natural environmental factors. We need to know the interdependence between fish stocks, the distribution of the stocks both vertically and horizontally at any given time, and when and where various fish species spawn. The minister has admitted in his speeches that we are not fully geared up in terms of research for a 200-mile zone. More trained people, more research vessels, and more laboratories are needed. I do not know of any place in the world where he has a better opportunity to get these things.
We have a million people unemployed. We have shipbuilders and scientists looking for work, and why does he not get on with the job? Despite his admission, the research and management budget for the Department of Fisheries and the Environ-
Fisheries
ment was increased by only 10 per cent to $21 million, and scientific manpower will be reduced by 16 for the budget year 1978-79.
The minister shakes his head. I stand to be corrected, because they are making alterations every day of the week. They have read the Gallup polls, and they know they are on the skids. They will now be digging into any pot they can find in order to raise some funds and establish some new programs. Some of the statistics which I am reporting and which come from the estimates books and other sources may be inaccurate in light of recent changes they have made in an effort to please fishermen-"please come back to the fold, please vote for us and please keep us in power."
This minister's attitude and the Liberal government's negative attitude to scientific research, I submit do not augur well for the future. This government has allowed expenditures to the foreign investment review agency to increase by 34.8 per cent and expenditures to the National Arts Centre to increase by 17.8 per cent. We are now subsidizing this organization for $10.4 million annually just "to see the show". Expenditures to the CBC have been increased by 11.8 per cent to $522 million, $10 million a week. This same government, however, cannot find sufficient additional money to carry out fisheries research.
We on this side believe that more fisheries research is essential for the future prosperity of the fisheries. We believe more money should be made available for research, and cutbacks in the above mentioned areas could provide these moneys. This viewpoint was also shared by the industry, for it was in evidence recently in the discussions held at the fisheries council meetings in Quebec.
Our commercial fish landings of 1,136,000 tons are less than one tenth of those of the leading producer of food from water, namely, Japan, which landed something like 10,620,000 tons. I am speaking from memory now and the minister can correct me, but I think we are sixteenth among the world's nations in so far as catching capability is concerned. Our catch represents approximately 2 per cent of world fisheries production. While these comparisons are interesting, they do not adequately describe the importance to Canada of food from water. It is more meaningful to say that many coastal regions are completely dependent on the commercial fisheries. It is more meaningful to say that a large scale production of a great variety of aquatic foods helps to meet the demand for protein in human diets.
We are seeing a shift of emphasis at present away from competitive exploitation of wild resources toward intensively managed fisheries resources. 1 believe that this gradual shift will continue, and in the long term aquaculture will play an ever-increasing role in the growth of fisheries. At present world production of fisheries from wild resources appears to be levelling off at about 70 million tons, while aquaculture, at six million tons, is still growing. Aquaculture is very important in many areas of Canada, and especially important to my colleague, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), who has told me that scallop fishermen in the Northumberland

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
Straits have some definite ideas for aquaculture development, if only the minister and his officials would consult and listen to them.
I believe that in the long run world trends in aquaculture will be followed in Canada, but to help bring this about we need a shift in our scientific program. Why, for example, should our scientific studies simply be a repeat of studies carried out by other countries? Surely, some effort should be made to have a quarterly, bi-annual, or annual scientific periodical prepared in which our scientific information on ocean studies and fisheries resources could be exchanged with friendly, co-operating nations.
To ensure that long-term research is not sacrificed for short-term needs, Canada needs a separate identity for fisheries research. We have had the Fisheries Research Board of Canada in operation for something like 75 years. I submit that now that we have taken over an area of the continental shelf one-third the size of Canada, the Fisheries Research Board and its activities must be reorganized and strengthened, and it should be encouraged to exchange fisheries data and facts with our friends internationally. Our bilateral agreements-I am sure the minister is well aware of this-cover this point, but 1 ask the minister are these agreements working? The machinery is there to hold scientific consultations with countries like Norway, Russia, Japan, Poland, Spain, and Portugal, to name but a few, but are these agreements operative?
I wish to turn now to another aspect of the Canadian fishing industry, namely, fleet development. I believe if we are to take full advantage of quota increases we need to start now on a program of rebuilding the Canadian fishing fleet. In the past, foreign fishing fleets often outfished Canadian vessels because of their modern equipment. In contrast, the newest vessels in the Canadian fleet are eight to nine years old, if we exclude the two scallop draggers that were launched only last week in Pictou.
Rebuilding the fleet was also a topic of discussion at the recent Liberal policy convention. Two resolutions were passed which urged, and I quote:
That the government direct financial assistance to expand the fishing industry, and
That the government participate in the program to make funding available for the building of new inshore fishing vessels. [DOT]
It will be interesting to see whether pressure from the Liberal rank and file will have any more impact or effect on the minister than the arguments of the Atlantic premiers and the fishing industry, and the arguments of the fishermen themselves. Obviously these well-meaning Atlantic Canada Liberals fired up the minister because he decided to tell them where they could go. Only four days after the Liberal convention, the minister, in a speech to the Herring Fishermens Marketing Cooperative, on March 2, in Saint John, New Brunswick, stated among other things:
The people who want to double the fleet are well meaning, they have just failed to examine the facts.
He also said that fleet expansion is only one of the mixed up ideas in the air. The minister has obviously picked up some rather bad habits from his leader, a leader who said to paraphrase him, that when members of parliament are five feet away from Parliament Hill they are nobodies. Obviously the Minister of Fisheries believes that when Liberal delegates are away from Ottawa they are nobodies and have mixed up ideas.
The minister's indifference not only applies to Liberal convention delegates, the so-called grass roots of his party, but applies as well to anyone who dares oppose him and his policies.
On April 26 the Halifax Chronicle-Herald carried a screaming headline on the front page-"Nova Scotia Has No Say In Policy", and the article read in part as follows;
The federal fisheries department has not honoured its pledge to seek more consultation and co-operation with the provincial fisheries department and local fishermen, fisheries minister Dr. Dan Reid said Tuesday.
Two days later the same Liberal provincial fisheries minister moved a resolution in the Nova Scotia legislature condemning the undue and harsh federal fisheries department regulations that were imposed, without consultation, on Nova Scotia fishermen. Finally, when these representations were ignored by the federal minister, Premier Gerald Regan, Canada's most western Liberal premier, sent a telegram to the Prime Minister protesting the arbitrary actions of the minister in the strongest possible terms. It is my understanding that the Prime Minister invited Mr. Regan to come to Ottawa to sit down with him and the Minister of Fisheries. It is also my understanding that Premier Regan told him where he could go, and it was not to Ottawa.
Last Friday we noticed that the usually genial minister was absent from his seat. He was dragged haltingly, grudgingly, belatedly, screaming down to Halifax to meet with Premier Regan where he finally agreed-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: That's not true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
The minister said that is not true. He had better argue that one with the press because there is a picture of him smiling with Premier Regan, on the front page of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. All is sweetness and light; all is honey and roses. The minister finally agreed to review his arbitrary regulations.
The minister cannot say he was uninformed of the fishermen's concerns. I and my colleagues in this House raised the matter on numerous occasions, and time and time again in committee. On April 28 at page 4971 of Hansard my question is recorded. I simply asked the minister to consult, rather than confront, Canada's fishermen. His response is a classic of arrogance and indifference. I could hardly believe my ears. The minister replied:
As for the complaint of the minister from Nova Scotia, I really must say that we cannot have negotiations with fishermen's groups, with processing groups and with provincial governments and then try to synchronize all of these every time we have to make a management decision. It is obvious that in the case of the management of the stocks the federal government, which is responsible-and, by

May 11, 1978

the way, which has to carry the can when there is a disaster-will continue to assume that responsibility, even if it means that at times provincial ministers are not satisfied.
So much for consultation. What colossal gall! This is nothing more than jackbooted, bully-boy, dictatorial tactics. It is "Alice in Wonderland" thinking. It is as if they say, "Everything we say, or order, or do, is right because we say it is right, and any one of you fellows who disagrees with us is nothing more than a separatist." That is what we get from the other side these days.
This minister and this government should know, but they have obviously forgotten, the primary rules and purpose of democracy. They have forgotten that they were elected to serve their fellowman-not elected to enslave him.
It was not only the premier of Nova Scotia who had to wire this minister. On May 9, Premier Bennett of British Columbia wired the Prime Minister and asked him to get with it through his Minister of Fisheries and help ease some of the problems on the west coast. This minister has consistently opposed the rebuilding of the Canadian Fishing fleet until quotas or stocks have fully recovered. He has stated in his speeches that a rebuilding program would put pressure on him to increase quotas prematurely. I say this need not happen if it were the Canadian share of the over-all quota which was increased at the expense of the foreign share and not an increase in the over-all quota. After all, Mr. Speaker, it was the minister who said that the foreign fleets would only be allowed to catch those fish which are "surplus to our needs".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
The minister says that is right. I say to him that by not building now the result will be the foreign fleets will make the greatest headway in future quota allocations.
I sometimes wonder if the right hand in this department knows what the left hand is doing. The minister's views on rebuilding the fleet are not shared, for example, by the federal Atlantic regional director general of the fisheries and marine service, Mr. Douglas Johnson. Last August when addressing over 150 delegates attending the Atlantic Fisheries technological conference in Halifax, Mr. Johnson is reported as stating that the development of non-traditional Fishing of such species as squid and silver hake will generate hundreds of onshore and offshore jobs in the Atlantic region. When making that statement Mr. Johnson knew that these soft species of Fish can only be caught with freezer trawlers. The minister's views on freezer trawlers are not shared by Mr. Eric Nowe, business agent for over 1,000 Nova Scotia Fishermen, who stated on Saturday, April 29, that the province's Fishery will go nowhere unless it expands into freezer trawler fishing of non-traditional species.
I believe we need to develop a Canadian capability in new Fish species, otherwise these species will always be surplus to our needs, available only to foreigners, and our people will continue to be unemployed. I believe that within the next Five years we need a minimum of Five freezer trawlers with the capability of catching and freezing species such as silver hake,
Fisheries
round nosed grenadiers, Argentine, squid, capelin, and offshore mackerel, which must be frozen as quickly as possible upon removal from the sea. Practically all of these species are presently being given away by this Liberal government under bilateral agreements as surplus to our needs.
The minister shakes his head. He should get together with his own officials. I raised this question in committee only last week. I wonder how many members of this House are aware of what we are talking about in weight? In reply to my question, Dr. May, director general of resource services, stated that Canadians have been allocated a quota on the Scotian Shelf of silver hake of 17,200 metric tonnes for 1977, which he admitted is a substantial amount in light of the fact that catches of this Fish are almost zero. Those are his words. If the minister does not like them, he can argue with his own officials. We have the same quota for 1978, and without a Canadian fleet of freezer trawlers our catch will again be zero. Dr. May also stated we have a quota of 1,000 tonnes of round nosed grenadier, a quota of 25,000 tonnes of squid, and an allocation of 60,000 tonnes of capelin. Anyone familiar with the fishing industry knows that in these figures lies a whole new industry for Atlantic Canada.
Dr. May went on to say that the difFiculty in acquiring a capacity to exploit these underexploited species is the presssure such an operation will put on the Fishing of more traditional stocks. What seems to be ignored is the fact that whenever we bring in foreign freezer trawlers under any arrangement in an effort to take some of these under-utilized species, we automatically put fishing pressure on the more traditional species, which appears to me to be a penny wise and pound foolish Fisheries policy. The quotas are there; they are allocated to Canada, so it only makes common sense to build at least a few freezer trawlers in order to capitalize on this resource.
The foreign fleets are obviously not as keen on conserving our Fish stocks as is the Minister of Fisheries. As he is well aware, there are rumours of "juggling" quotas within our 200-mile limit. There is also an apparent escalation of fishing effort just outside the 200-mile limit by countries which may be flying flags of convenience.
There are reports of Mexican, Venezuelan, and possibly Spanish flags in evidence just on the fringe of our 200-mile zone, and their operations may well not be in accordance with rules laid down by the International Commission for North Atlantic Fisheries prior to the implementation of NAFO, the organization which replaced ICNAF.
We must ask ourselves what this new threat does to fish stocks that cross over the 200-mile zone and why we are so reticent in providing new job opportunities in the fisheries for Canadians. According to all reports, many people in Atlantic Canada are still looking for work. In April the seasonally adjusted Figure for the Atlantic area was 13.2 per cent. I submit that construction of some freezer trawlers would provide meaningful employment, ashore and afloat, for some of these people.

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
The minister has pointed out that the government does have a fishing vessel subsidy program for new vessel construction and refits. However, the budget for this program has remained constant over the past several years, while inflation has sent vessel costs skyward. Clearly, the funding is inadequate. That is why we have proposed the establishment of a fisheries development fund from which grants and loans would be made available for ship refits as well as for new vessel construction by the inshore fleet or for freezer trawlers.
On shore, this fund could provide assistance for the construction of freezers or holding depots for fish. By being able to freeze more fish, processing plants could operate year round, providing needed employment in our maritime regions.
It is obvious, when looking at the 1977 landings, that steps must be taken immediately to capitalize on all our fisheries resources. According to preliminary statistics for 1977, and if these are not correct I hope the minister will update them, fish landings showed a tremendous dip from 1976. For Canada as a whole, fish landings dropped by 37 per cent, from 2.4 billion pounds in 1976 to 1.7 billion in 1977.
In yet another field, the boundary problems on both coasts are yet to be resolved. On Georges Bank, we urged the government to consider seriously a joint management scheme with the United States. The Atlantic premiers and New England governors agreed to such a scheme in June, 1977, but unfortunately to date this matter is unresolved.
In still another area, if fishermen are to benefit from increased catches, our marketing efforts have to improve. We should and we can expand our markets in other world areas, specifically in Europe and Japan. The Japanese are anxious to buy more fish since they have lost vast areas in which they formerly fished prior to the extension of the 200-mile limit. Mitsunori Yoshida, a representative of Japanese fisheries, says the Canadian fishery offers a great hope for his countrymen who annually consume ten million metric tonnes of seafood. This offers a tremendous challenge to Canadian entrepreneurs.
It must be obvious from what I have said that I believe there are great opportunities being offered today by the fishing industry. However, it is obvious, I also believe, that in order for the industry to achieve its full potential there must be clear-cut, long range government policies which will permit the individual fisherman, the entrepreneur, and the private sector to plan properly for its development.
I have stated a number of important areas where I believe government policies are incorrect, unclear or non-existent. As a result of this situation there is a feeling of inertia and uncertainty throughout the entire industry which has significantly diminished the ability of the private sector to plan ahead, and to secure the benefits which should be available to stimulate the Atlantic economy.
We on this side believe that control over the fishing industry must be retained by the federal government. However, in carrying out the many functions that go with this responsibility, such as establishing the total allowable catch, the allocations for the inshore fishermen, the offshore fishermen and
foreign vessels, the issuing of fishing licences, and assistance in rebuilding the fleet, to name but a few functions, there is no reason whatever for the lack of consultation with the provinces on these matters which have a vital impact on their local economy and their way of life.
The federal government must assume an important role in the over-all development of the Canadian fishing industry. However, the industry is like a diamond, with many facets, It has many aspects whose development can best be carried out by the private sector. While I believe the government should improve its surveillance and coastguard capabilities, I do not believe, as a supporter of free enterprise, that the government should own or operate processing, handling, or cold storage facilities.
Government should not become engaged directly in marketing fish products or in the operation of commercial fishing vessels. These activities should remain-

When the minister states that he and his government intend to play more than a supportive role in these fields, he simply compounds the uncertainty created by his own government's lack of policy.
What the fishermen and the industry are crying out for today is a clear statement that the government does not intend to intervene in the areas which I mentioned and that it will stick primarily to its support role.
A supporting role should not only cover a policy of investment allowances or tax remission when freezer trawlers are built, but the Income Tax Act should be used to stimulate a policy of fleet replacement. Some of our shipyards are already dosed and the valuable skills of the shipbuilders, once lost, are not easily replaced. So that our inshore, as well as our offshore fishermen can plan ahead, we need a policy for licensing inshore and offshore vessels which will maintain some balance in the catching capacities of these two segments of the industry.
In areas where there are definite signs that the inshore fleet is growing, where there are father and son teams, and where the small local communities are almost entirely dependent on the fishery, policy must be established which will ensure that the opportunities for growth in those areas are recognized.
This government should realize that equipment used at sea, on salt water, deteriorates very quickly. Fishermen should therefore be permitted not only a regular write-off of ships and

May 11, 1978

equipment, but a special allowance which could be used towards the cost of replacement. If this policy were followed, the industry could generate a much larger amount of the capital required for fleet replacement and it would be less difficult tc secure investors throughout Atlantic Canada for the construction of inshore and offshore ships.
Since the present minister and this government have not come forward with any progressive policies along the lines 1 have mentioned, I have moved, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That this House condemns the federal Minister of Fisheries for his failure tc consult and co-operate with provincial Fisheries ministers and Fishermen prior to establishing arbitrary rules and regulations which are harmful to the Fishermen, and for his failure to develop a positive policy for the protection and development of the Canadian Fishing industry in order to derive maximum advantage for Canadians from the extended jurisdiction.

As for my meeting with Premier Regan, the actual picture belies the "screaming and kicking" image which the hon. member used. Fisheries
The hon. member opposite has placed a motion before us which takes me to task for my so-called failure to consult and co-operate with provincial fisheries ministers and fishermen. If I have failed to do either, the hon. member from South Shore and myself are using different dictionaries.

They show that the mechanisms for consultation are not only in place but are being utilized.
I could give many more examples which burst the bubble of the motion placed before us, but I shall not ask the indulgence of the House while I go thicugh the list. It would take up my allotted time, and more. Instead, I wish, with your permission, to table documents which outline those mechanism for consultation and co-operation-some 28 pages for consultation in Canada alone, including, of course, examples of the types of meetings in which I have been engaged over the months.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing these facts to be put on the record. They are important. There are many mechanisms for consultation which are available affecting provincial governments, various sectors of the industry, processors, fishermen, and other interested parties.
As I have said and documented, Mr. Speaker, consultation between all aspects of the fishing industry is an ongoing and valued aspect of the management of this nation's fishery by this government. Not only are we engaging in consultation but we are making sure that the department is as close as possible to the fishermen.
I wish to touch briefly on the degree of decentralization of the fisheries management of the regions. Since I assumed

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
responsibility for the fisheries in 1974, my department has moved increasingly toward further delegation of authority for fisheries management to regional fisheries. I am proud to point out with respect to the fisheries component of the department that more than 94 per cent of the personnel work in areas outside the national capital region. The Treasury Board task force on decentralization indicates that this is one of the most decentralized organizations in the federal government. Not only have we decentralized our personnel, we have given them the necessary authority to take decisions and to react to problems on the spot.
In the last five years we have established regional directors-general in six major Canadian fisheries regions. These positions are staffed by competent senior executives who are in close touch with the fishing industry. Reporting to them in many locations are area managers who, again, are given responsibility for taking local decisions.
I am personally very proud of another decentralization measure which I instituted. It is the appointment of community service officers who live and work in fishing villages. These officers work closely with fishermen interpreting federal fisheries policy and regulations, helping them cut through red tape and, equally important, feeding in their point of view. I think these are all examples of effective consultation.
But in accepting and encouraging the consultative process I must also keep in mind another truth, that is, the reality that consultation is no guarantee for unanimity. We might as well resign ourselves to the fact that there will always be competing interests and objectives. The federal authority for fisheries is the clearing house for these divergent views, the mediator for conflicting opinion and, ultimately, the decision maker. The federal authority also carries the can if things go wrong, and I did not hear the provinces yelling too loudly to join in when the going was rough. Decisions have to be made somewhere, by someone, and I, sir, not the hon. member opposite nor the president of a provincial fishermen's association, nor even a provincial minister of fisheries, have to make those decisions. And I have to answer for those decisions in this very House. The constitution clearly places that responsibility in my hands and I believe, without reflection on my person, that this responsibility is placed as it should be.
As all members of the House are aware, a great deal of time and energy is spent in resolving boundary and quota disputes between ourselves and our neighbours to the south. I am frankly less eager to see that same time and energy being expended at the provincial level.
If fish grew roots I would be willing to give a fair shake to the argument some provinces are currently expounding that they should have a greater role in decision-making affecting fisheries management. Fish, Mr. Speaker, are not trees. And for the converse reason, forestry is not a federal responsibility. Some stock, for example the Atlantic salmon, migrate past five provinces. If we were to hand those five provinces five knives- or perhaps I should say five fishing poles-to divide up that resource, I am afraid their five hooks might end up in each other's eyes.
There can be no movement from the premise that the common property of the living resources of the sea requires federal management. That does not preclude, and the documents I have tabled prove we have not precluded, the important role of the provinces in working with the federal government or their role in relation to the processing industry, in education and training for fisheries, and in matters such as providing good roads and water supplies to serve the fish plants.
An encouraging, positive step in that vein is the increased recognition of fisheries in some recent provincial budgets. In addition, shared optimism toward the future of the fisheries appeared clearly at the first ministers' economic conference in February where, for the first time, fisheries was included among the sectors of the economy to be discussed and became publicly identified as a major and growing sector of the economy.
This same confidence is also evident in the decision of this government to restore fisheries to its rightful place as a separate government department, a move, I am pleased to note, which was greeted enthusiastically by hon. members opposite. I hope, now that that other decision has been taken, we can move diligently to bring forward the legislation.
Let me touch for a moment on just what it is we have to be enthusiastic about. The fishery today represents a billion dollar industry which in the last four years has increased its production value by 55 per cent, increased its export value by 65 per cent, and taken control of 630,000 square miles of resources, which means it can double its supply of raw material. Today's fisherman is earning an income 50 per cent higher, in real terms, than he could ten years ago.
We are at last approaching the day when we can say that Canada's oldest industry is one of its best. An industry formerly fraught with instability and low return can, if we sensibly and carefully develop the management regime to reap the best benefit from extended jurisdiction, become one of the maint-stays of this nation's economy. We must, however, not be blinded by this bright future before us. We must not forget the lessons learned from past mistakes. Time and time again high hopes, messages of promises and zealous enthusiasm, have seduced us into grand failures. This is what we must avoid in fisheries. No one wants to add the 200-mile zone to the list of broken hopes.
There is no doubt in my mind that the sure way to shatter that hope is not to have a national approach in developing policies and management of a national resource. We will only avoid discord, costly collisions and fragmentation of effort, by a common acceptance and sensitivity to a goal which is wider than provincial boundaries and local considerations.
I have to say that the so-called current difficulty with the provinces is much more evident in reading newspapers and listening to the hon. member for South Shore and the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) than it is in my

May 11, 1978

personal dealings with my provincial colleagues or with fishermen.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: You don't deal with them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
The cries we are hearing today for increasing provincial responsibility for fisheries management were not heard when prospects for the industry were bleak. This is really a case where victory has many fathers, and defeat is an orphan.
Our final goal, which must not be lost sight of, is simple. It is to make fishing a profession which will be as attractive to the next generation as it is starting to be to our own. It is to create a self-sustaining industry which can give to its fishermen the benefits enjoyed by all other organized professions in our society, which is security of income and security of employment. It is to give the shareholders of the companies involved a reasonable expectation of return on their investment and, foremost, to give the coastal communities-the small coastal communities-in whose name we argued for the 200-mile zone, the assurance that they will be served first.
We must assure them that their needs will be met first and that the right of the many will not be sacrificed for the privilege of the few. There are, by the way, some sure-fire ways of ensuring that the inshore fisherman, who deserves the most from extended jurisdiction, is going to get the least. Let us look, for example, at the much touted plans for fleet expansion. No doubt, to handle the increased ground fish on the Atlantic coast we will have to have replacements for some of the aging sectors of the fleet, and eventually, with stocks recovering, perhaps some expansion, but 1 do not see the need for panic button expansion. Between 1959 and 1974 the tonnage of larger Atlantic vessels over 50 gross tons multiplied by five, that is, increased by 500 per cent. The Atlantic catch of all species went up only about 10 per cent. The little old fleet of the 1950s was catching almost the same amount of fish because there were more fish to catch.
The present ground fish fleet of larger vessels has the capacity to take half again its present catch and provide better incomes, if we increase the number of fish in the water and if we increase the catch rates. If we do it the other way around, that is, increase the fleet first, we are like a man looking over his exhausted woodlot who, instead of planting more trees, is spending his money on more chain saws to cut the shrubs.
There are opportunities for expansion in fishing capelin, silver hake, Argentine, and grenadier, the so-called under-utilized species. Federal subsidy and licensing policies are geared to encourage diversification into these species, but I can only reiterate what I told the hon. member for South Shore yesterday in this chamber, and that is that the economics of fishing these species seem to attract the Canadian industry about as much as fishing for sun fish or sea cucumbers. The day may come for silver hake and the like, as it came for the lobster we once used to fertilize our fields. In fact there are some signs that we can develop under-utilized species, as we have done with squid for the past couple of years, but the fact is that my desk is not overloaded with applications for licences-which I
Fisheries
would grant-to catch those underutilized species which our industry has not always found economic to catch.
I know that some people, mostly from outside the fishing industry itself, are impatient with the cautious federal approach to fleet expansion, but have reasons for this approach. We have bitter memories of disasters as a result of over-hasty developments, and I cite herring on both coasts as an example. There are also good examples of fleet development which resulted from private initiative working in a good framework. The salmon fleet and the herring fleet on the west coast are good examples of organized and well disciplined development.
I might add with regard to the progress we are seeing in the 200-mile zone that we have a dramatic salmon enhancement program. This program will double the present level of the catch on the west coast. It gained cabinet approval because it promised money and profits for Canada and for it fishermen, plant workers, and the industry in general. These profits have been based on holding the line on over-expansion in fleets or over-expansion in processing to avoid dissipating the gains that were made.
The simple argument against holus-bolus expansion of our fleet is to examine what improved catch rates on our existing fishing vessels will mean for fishermen. They are who we are here to serve, and I see no faster road to disaster for them than to forget the very simple rule of thumb that biology cannot keep up with technology and that the wealth of the oceans cannot yet match the greed of man.
I have made my position very clear on many occasions. We have before us the opportunity to become one of the world's largest exporters of fish products by value, or the owner of the largest fish warehouses in the world. That is one of the reasons we attach great importance to marketing. We have to recognize that Canadians fish for dollars rather than for food supplies. The extension of fisheries jurisdiction by Canada and many other nations has brought major structural changes in world markets, and Canada's need for new and expanded markets, both for traditional and non-traditional species, clearly necessitates national policies and initiatives.
I want to take this opportunity to commend the formation of the Canadian Association of Fish Exporters, which will become known as CAFE, and of the British Columbia Seafoods Group.

speechtext:
I would prefer it if the hon. member would put his question at the conclusion of my remarks, although I am in the hands of the House. But if he does not object, I would prefer him to put his question at the end.

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
As I was saying, 1 commend the creation of an association of processors in a marketing organization, and I expressed the same satisfaction with the creation of the west coast group. The more market intelligence, promotion, and development I see, the more positive I will be about the future of this industry. The federal government has helped to instigate CAFE, and to see the positive results of its marketing effort will be most reassuring. But our interest does not stop there. We will keep an eye on this organization to see where we can assist it. It may be that eventually we will ask parliament to help it, as other nations have helped their marketing organization, with a legal framework.
There is just not enough time for me to touch on all the examples that are available to show the extent of the federal government's involvement in this industry. Such an overview would quickly and effectively dispel any truth there is in the words contained in the motion which prompted this debate, that there is not a positive policy for the protection and development of the Canadian fishing industry to derive maxium advantage for Canadians from the extended jurisdiction.
Let us look at some of the facts. In 1974 Canada took 34 per cent of all fish caught off her Atlantic coast. In 1978 Canada has 53 per cent of the total allowable catch, and most of the remainder is non-traditional species, such as capelin.
In 1974 Canada took 34 per cent of traditional groundfish, such as cod and haddock. That figure has risen to 69 per cent of the total allowable catch in 1978 inside and outside the 200-mile zone. When we allow for allocations to the United States and the French islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, and for allocations of stock either exclusively beyond 200 miles or straddling the boundary, foreign nations have only 13 per cent of the traditional groundfish, and those allocations are almost entirely in the northern areas.
I think I must inject some realism into what has already been said by the hon. member for South Shore, and no doubt what will be said by other opposition members as this debate continues.
We must face the future of the fishing industry with all our expectations in line with our opportunities. There must be a balance between the vested interested within and between provinces. I think I have been very tolerant amidst the swirl of misinformation and opportunistic public statements which have been coming at me and my department over the past months.

speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. It is a small point of order. The minister has just been giving figures for 1978. It is my impression that we are now at May 11, 1978. I wonder how he can produce figures for 1978 at this point in the year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
I am afraid I did not quite understand the hon. member's question. The allocation between nations, between fleet types, etc., are set a year in advance in the fishing plan which was triggered on January I,
1978.1 will check in case I misinformed the hon. member and I will obviously put the facts on the record.
Perhaps the hon. member for South Shore has done me a favour by presenting his motion today, thus giving me the opportunity to set the record straight.
I need only turn to the controversy over the seal harvest to cite an example of where the tide was turned on misinformation. I can only say to those who would see themselves as the Brian Davies of the Atlantic fisheries, that they should be prepared to have their arguments stand up to close scrutiny.
I am willing to consult, as I indicated before. I think the paper I have tabled showed that I am willing to consult. I am consulting, but I ask that those with whom I deal understand the federal position. Because fish laugh at borders, federal fisheries must cross those borders. When many interests are at play, being responsible to all means you can never satisfy all. Trying to do so-trying to tell everyone what they want to hear, and granting every request-would be the end of our hopes for management of the fisheries.
Sometimes the decision that is best for all is bitter to the few; that is sad but is unavoidable. The lesson of history is that fisheries management never takes care of itself; it needs management that makes sense on an over-all level. To the provincial spokesman arguing for more jurisdiction over fishing, I can answer that I will not abdicate lightly the power given by the constitution, the same power that in the last four years enabled the federal government to take such strong action in getting the 200 mile limit and in rescuing and reinvigorating major sectors of the industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
I might mention also the attitude I sometimes encounter, that consultation with the provinces should mean automatic adoption of their views, even when their individual views differ, for example, the jealous claims to reserve all the fish migrating near a province for that province, a claim that flies in the face of every principle of national unity or of sensible management of the fishing industry.
Recently I read in the Financial Post someone's remark that fish did not come from Ottawa, it came from God. I do not know what fisheries act applies up there, but I do know my responsibility as custodian of the resources of the seas on behalf of the people of Canada, and I intend to maintain clearly the lines of responsibility. The fish belong to the people of Canada and are managed and allocated on their behalf by a department responsible to this parliament. The fishermen are licensed to catch the fish. I see them as being free to sell fish with a minimum of constraint and a maximum of organization to protect their interests, but I see constraints, for example, as no wholesale selling over the side without some processing in Canada. I see the processors as making their own decisions as to processing the raw material they bought and selling it on the open market, again only with such constraints as will be in the interests of the whole country.

May 11, 1978

Fisheries have become a bit of a bandwagon. Sometimes I suspect that if fishing and fisheries could survive when few governments were interested, except for the federal government, and when many people ignored their existence, it may survive this renewed interest when there are many people who would like to take over the wheel of the wagon. My colleagues, especially my parliamentary secretary and others, will cover other aspects of the fisheries. I am thinking in particular of the international dimension and of inland waters. The fact remains that my predecessor of many years ago-I am flattered to have been compared to him at one time-the Hon. Jim Sinclair, once said this is a great portfolio and he would have no other. After three and a half years in charge of that portfolio, and despite our differences of views at times, I still think that this is a fabulous portfolio and I would not ask for any other for a good time to come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) has rendered a useful service to the House by presenting a motion which permits a discussion on the fishing industry. The fishing industry is becoming an increasingly important factor in the economy of Canada.
The Canadian fishing industry is geographically divided between the Atlantic coast and the Pacific coast. Consequently, the New Democratic Party has had a member from the Atlantic coast on the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond
5330

Fisheries

Not only has he been a very active member of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, but he has attended various international conferences on the law of the sea. He has played a very useful role in this regard. Unfortunately the hon. member for New Westminster had a commitment in his own constituency. I make no pretension whatsoever at being an expert on fisheries, nor have I ever been a member of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, but I have spent many, many hours sitting on the docks and talking to the fishermen of my constituency. I have travelled a good many miles with them through the Gulf of Georgia, the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and up into some of the northern waters. Therefore I have had many opportunities to talk with them and listen to their complaints. I want to say to the minister that these fishermen have complaints. Fishermen like farmers are not born bel-lyachers. They do not tend to complain all the time. Most of the time they accept the vicissitudes of life with great equanimity. I have listened to their complaints and have attempted to pass them on to the minister.
The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) is one of the more competent ministers in the government. speechtext:
I have always found him approachable and willing to listen to reason. He is a great improvement on some of the ministers of fisheries and the environment we have had. Certainly he inherited a sorry mess. Some of the things I will say are not said as a direct reflection on him, but on a lack of policy over a good many years. However, the minister ought not to take too much comfort out of statistics, as he tended to do this afternoon. He spoke about the incomes of fishermen being 50 per cent higher than they were ten years ago. If the minister will take the trouble to look at the cost of fuel for ships, buying ships, licences, operating ships, and the cost of living, which has risen a great deal more than 50 per cent over the last ten years, he will find that the real incomes of fishermen have not kept pace with the general state of conditions in the economy as a whole.
Briefly, I should like to enumerate some of the complaints I have received from fishermen in my constituency. The first complaint deals with the boat licensing system which was inaugurated by Mr. Jack Davis. I remember when it happened.
I remember hon. members of the New Democratic Party took strong exception to it. Our objection was based on a number of

grounds. Our first ground was that it was not being done by an act of parliament and there were no regulations. One of the difficulties with the Department of Fisheries and the Environment is that so much of the actions taken by the department are passed on to the public through press releases, ministerial statements, and ministerial orders. Very little of the actions are in the form of regulations passed under an act which can be examined minutely, so that a person knows with certainty what his or her rights are. That is one complaint we had about the licensing system. It is still true that there is a very vague area surrounding the entire area of boat licensing.
We objected to the boat licensing system when it was inaugurated because we were convinced that it would develop a trade in licences, that licences would become commodities. Certainly that is true. Every other week end when I return to my constituency, fishermen or young men who want to become fishermen are in my constituency office telling me of the fabulous figures they have to pay to buy a licence. It almost costs as much now to buy a licence as it does to buy a boat. Virtually this precludes many young men from getting into the fishing business at all. 1 realize the objective was to keep down the number of people in the fishing industry because of conservation. That was understandable, but I should like to say that it was rendered on the basis of the pocketbook, and it has not worked satisfactorily.
The worst criticism when the plan was introduced, and it is being demonstrated every day, was that it would lead to an increasing concentration of fishing in the hands of a smaller and more elite group and eventually into the hands, in large measure, of the fish processing industry. There is a good deal of dissatisfaction with reference to both licensing systems. There is a good deal of need for either the fisheries committee of the House or a task force to re-examine it and put it in proper legislative form in such a way that there is not this trading in licences.
The second complaint I get from the fishermen in my constituency is that we are being out-manoeuvred in our talks with the American negotiators regarding our fishing rights. They feel, and I must say that I share their feelings, that our attitude in negotiating with the United States has a cap-inhand posture about it. I noticed that even in the discussions in the House on Monday when my colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), and myself yesterday, were asking questions about whether or not we should make it clear to the President of the United States that if the Americans are not going to carry out their commitments under the proposed reciprocal temporary agreement, Canada will have no choice but to follow a similar course of action.
Immediately the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talks about threats. Surely it is not a threat to say if two parties have reached an agreement, and one party decides to renege on that agreement, it is no longer in effect as far as the other party is concerned. All we are asking is that the Americans be reminded that the proposition works both ways, but we are accused of
May 11, 1978

trying to threaten the Americans the moment we ask the government to stand up and make it clear that we Canadians have rights as well.
The minister in reply to a question from the leader of this party last Monday about retaliation said that it should be noted that last year when the Americans put some restriction on our fishermen we reacted by keeping their shrimp boats out of our waters. It is true that the government stopped the shrimp fishing off Tofino last year for the American fishermen, but it is equally true that we stopped it for the Canadian fishermen when conservation restrictions were placed on shrimp fishing so that on the grounds of conservation they could say to the United States that "neither of them are fishing and we are not really retaliating".
There has been a series of retreats in this whole matter of negotiating fishing rights as between the United States fishermen and the Canadian fishermen. I would like to remind the House that we once had a fish war between Canada and the United States. This afternoon the minister referred to Mr. James Sinclair, who was one of the best ministers of fisheries we have ever had in Canada. In the 1940s when he was minister of fisheries the Americans decided to fish very heavily on the fish that normally go up the Fraser River. Mr. Sinclair ordered all the west coast fishing boats in the Strait of Juan de Fuca to intercept the fish which would normally be going to American waters, and it did not take very long for the Americans to realize that it was not a very productive kind of confrontation. The result was that they came to their senses and began talking business. I can still remember Mr. Sinclair's statement to the effect "We do not want this fish war, but when you plead and ask and request and get no answer, then you have no recourse but to take some steps."
All the fishermen are really asking for is a feeling that we are prepared to stand up and fight for them, not to be belligerent or to ask for more than we are entitled to, but just not to be pushed around. We have an example right now in this 1978 proposed interim agreement. It is the height of absurdity when we, by executive order, announce an agreement which has not yet been ratified by the United States Congress, leaving the whole proposal open to court action by any group in that country. This is what has happened. The report is that the United States west coast fishermen have told the United States Senate committee that they propose to drop the charges on the understanding that the United States officials will not allow Canadians to expand into more salmon trolling areas off the United States west coast as is promised and proposed in the Canadian-U.S. 1978 agreement. I do not know whether the American government will give them that concession, but if they do I assume that our Minister of Fisheries will stipulate that what we gave under the 1978 agreement will also be set aside.
Surely there must be a better way to work out relations between the two countries with respect to fisheries other than to have Canada in the ridiculous position of having by executive order agreed to a certain policy only to find that the policy is not effective because it has not been ratified by the United
Fisheries
States Congress. If we are going to accept an agreement with the Americans, then that agreement ought to come into effect only when it has been ratified and we would not be placed in the ridiculous position which we are in at the present time.
The fishermen do not know where they are at. On Monday the halibut season opens, and the representatives of the Department of Fisheries have told the fishermen on the west coast to go up to the Alaskan waters to fish, and hope that the Americans do not raise any objections. However, as long as the interim agreement has not been passed by congress there is nothing to prevent anybody from getting an injunction to stop them. This is a very embarrassing situation and a very clumsy way in which to carry on negotiations between the two countries because, if the Americans insist on going back to the 1978 interim agreement, it will mean our fishermen will not be able to do salmon trolling in the waters off the coast of Washington. Or if they do it will be in an area which was restricted by the agreement reached last year to allow the Americans more offshore area in return for the fact that they are giving more inshore area to their native Indians.
This was a bad decision, and many of the fishermen's organizations argue that it lost them 40 per cent of their potential catch. I am not in a position to say whether that is accurate or not. What bothers them most is that they keep insisting they have never been consulted about this. It is true they are asked to come to meetings in Ottawa or that a meeting is held in Vancouver and they are told a few things there, but the real decision about the final agreement has only come to them after the fact.
In the time I have left, Mr. Speaker, let me say that the thing that is causing the fishermen the most concern at the present time is the question of the negotiation of fishing boundaries with the United States. I tried to follow the negotiations and I have to say that I think the Canadian government, to use the language of the street, has "blown" this matter of boundaries. Canadian negotiators are taking the legalistic position of the equidistant line, whereas the United States is arguing for the maximum or trench system, which I understand they are arguing against on the east coast. The minister will say that the position we are taking is without prejudice. That is a good lawyer's position, but everyone who has ever negotiated knows perfectly well that when you go before an arbitration board it will not just look at the documentation but at the positions the two parties took originally. If they have to look at the trench proposal and the equidistant line proposal we will have already lost a good deal of the fishing potential to which we think we are entitled.
We fear there is a strong possibility that the boundary line will be brought down as far as Hecate Strait and Dixon Entrance. If it is, it will deny west coast fishermen of a good deal of the area upon which they have depended for their livelihood.
I hope that sometime soon the minister will tell the House the extent to which the fishermen's organizations on the west

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
coast have had an opportunity to contribute some input to these negotiations regarding boundaries. I do not mean being asked to a meeting and given a free lunch-I mean a real input about the extent of meetings with Mr. Cadieux and having someone sitting in on the discussions, or even in an anteroom, who could be consulted during the discussions. This is important to them. It is their livelihood, and not just for today or tomorrow but for the years ahead.
I conclude by saying to the minister that if he were to listen to the message from the fishermen who ply the waters of the Pacific coast he would hear them saying they want more consultation, they want to feel they have his ear, that they have access to the Canadian negotiator who is determining what their fishing areas will be in the future. They want consultation, Mr. Speaker.

Before discussing the hon. member's motion I would like to make a few remarks about the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), not because he is not competent, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) suggested earlier, but because he is a man I admire, a loyal and open man and I am convinced that he gives a lot of his time for the advancement of fisheries in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not like at all to leave on the record an assertion which may not be accurate and this is why, further considering the problem of the relations with one province in particular, I should say that we were invited to send the deputy minister who, unfortunately, was held by another meeting.
