speechtext:
I thank the minister for his explanations. Of course, as he will recognize himself we had some reason to know why the representatives of his department were not there. 1 thank him.
Mr. Speaker, this criticism goes in the same direction- except for the one relating to the representation in Gaspe-as the motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), as he also deplores the lack of co-operation and consultation between the federal government and its provincial counterparts. Although the 200-mile zone limit is an unprecedented asset for the eastern part of the country in particular, it seems to me we should establish at any cost a global policy, a policy of cohesion involving both the provincial and federal governments. I am convinced of the minister's dedication to the development of fisheries in Canada but it appears clearly to me that we do not draw all the benefits we should from the extension of our fishing limit to 200 miles. For example, for 1977, when the 200-mile limit was introduced, our catch for all species in the Atlantic area were only 58 per cent. As far as the catch of so-called traditional species is concerned, namely those we fish intensively, the figure was 76 per cent, which is an increase over 1976 of only 14 per cent. I seems very low to me.
The minister has announced to the House that for the current year foreign quotas would be almost exclusively made
May 11, 1978

up of species which we do not exploit much such as silver hake, capelin, silver-fish, roughnose grenadier and so on. I am quite happy that foreign involvement in our traditional fisheries in Canada has been almost eliminated but we should make a breakthrough in fishing for the non traditional species which I have just mentioned. Those resources belong to us and I think that diversifying our fishing products would help stabilize that industry.
Of course, successful management of our fisheries requires that we make sound decisions on exploitation and preservation of stocks. One just has to look how herring has been overexploited on our coasts to realize it. So we must tread softly and not repeat past mistakes. That is why we cannot let foreigners exploit some species because we have no ship equipped for that kind of fisheries or there is no substantial demand for those species. At that state, it is up to government agencies to promote catching of less known species in assisting fishermen who would to get involved in this fishery, in finding markets and in stimulating the domestic demand with advertising and information campaigns. We do that already for dairy products and eggs, so why not for fish? I realize also that from January to September 1977 we imported quantities of codfish, salmon, silver-fish, herring, crab, lobster and some other species which are abundant within our waters and that such imports amounted to close to $70 million.
Is this situation due to bad marketing or bad forecasts? It should be noted that these species are fished mostly in the Atlantic, in our waters, and that they come back to us as finished products. Mr. Speaker, $70 million is not a sum to be taken lightly, especially in an area like the Gaspe peninsula. It is therefore imperative not only to ensure our share of foreign markets, but also to protect our domestic market because of the present level of competition on world markets.
I believe that to take advantage of the increased stocks of groundfish on the Atlantic coast, we should refit our fishing fleet, which is becoming rather obsolete. In this regard, I am concerned by the fact that Quebec received nothing under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act between July 1977 and December 1977. It is necessary to offer good credit facilities to allow our fishermen to equip themselves for new fisheries outside our traditional fishing industry and to allow them at the same time to remain the owners of their boats. Finally, we should improve the lot of our inshore fishermen who have been hurt in the past by the depletion of the cod stocks. I am happy that in 1978 the inshore fishermen will receive 80 per cent of the cod quotas in Canada. This is a step in the right direction.
Sea fishery in Quebec provides employment for about 100 communities along the Gaspe coast, on the north shore and in the Magdalen Islands. It provides employment for nearly 6,500 fishermen and just under 1,500 people in processing plants. Unfortunately, there now exist certain difficulties, including smaller catches and aging of the fleet. It is therefore important for my area that in the next few years there should
Fisheries
be a development policy to increase and stabilize the income of fishermen as well as employment in the sectors of processing and marketing.
I therefore ask the minister not to favour certain areas of the Atlantic region at the expense of others. It seems to me that the Gaspe peninsula has suffered enough from the indifference of governments as concerns its economic problems. The Gaspe people must have their share. Mr. Speaker, even though the minister has in general showed great interest in helping our fishermen develop a prosperous industry, it still remains that there is a lot to be done to guarantee that our resources will not be unduly exploited by foreigners at our expense. The sea is a reservoir of countless resources and will remain our great strength if we learn to preserve and develop systematically those resources.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) that as far as the staff is concerned, it is still difficult for the employees of the Department of Fisheries and Environment to work in their native tongue, especially on account of their low percentage of representation, that is 13 per cent, as well as the low rate of bilingualism among English-speaking employees, as mentioned in the last report of the Commissioner of Official Languages. Consequently, I would urge the minister to cope with the linguistic inequality by increasing the percentage of French-speaking employees to a fairer level to provide better services to French Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have had the opportunity to second this particular motion today because it gives me another opportunity, unfortunately an opportunity that we have to come back on again and again, to underline the shortcomings of this government. I regret that we have to return so often to a theme in the fisheries-environment area with which we have dealt on numerous occasions before, that is, the government's inadequacies.
Since the government persists in disregarding advice offered to it, suggestions made from this side of the House, smug and satisfied that its own ways are best, I have no alternative but to return to the charge, because I am satisfied from some of the borrowings that have come from the policies enunciated on this side that those policies are the correct ones. Furthermore, in other areas, notably in criminal justice, the Post Office and the economy, this government has proceeded on its own course, smug and satisfied that its own ways are best, in total disregard of the advice offered to it from this side of the House and from a somewhat less subjective perspective. Look at the results: a crime rate that makes Canadians, even here in Ottawa, uneasy about going out at night. We read reports daily in the newspapers and hear them over the air. We have a Post Office where morale is so low that the mail is being delivered in an offhanded, negligent manner, and an economy that has about as much resilience as a flat tire.

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
Today we hear of a third theory of ministerial responsibility enunciated by the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Mar-chand). Aside from the present minister, to whom I give a fair amount of credit, what makes us feel that this government is going to act any better as a government in this area than it has in any of the others? In these circumstances it is the opposition which, though without the power to change the direction, is called upon to point in the direction to which we should be heading. It is up to us to set the gyro in this desert land where landmarks are so few, and get the caravan of state moving toward a predetermined destination.
There is one feature of the government's failure to govern which imposes a certain restraint upon responsible critics such as I happen to think I am. In the circumstances now prevailing, at this very moment when negotiations have reopened in Ottawa to determine the rights and responsibilities of Canadian and American fishermen on the west coast, it is extremely difficult to underline the longstanding failure of the administration to prepare itself for the burden which would result from this assumption of responsibility, if only for fisheries management, for the 200 mile zone. I do not want to weaken the bargaining hand of the Canadian negotiatior at this critical juncture. I know what problems he is facing, what odds. But it is the fault of the government for failing to provide him with sound and credible grounds from which to bargain.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) mentioned the government's failure to put some backbone into the negotiating team. I maintain that it ought to have been put there ten or 15 years ago when the 200-mile limit was looming before us. But what do we find? We find that the enforcement machinery is not in place. There is no sign of its being put in place even today. Ought it to come as a surprise, then, that there should be an injunction from the American courts preventing Canadians from deriving benefit from an interim agreement?
I wanted to ask a couple of questions today. I wanted to know whether the government intends to accept any dilution of the rights agreed upon under that interim agreement. After all, an interim agreement is, nevertheless, an agreement. We understood it was an agreement. The Americans, apparently, do not think it is until it has been ratified. Is the government prepared to assure us that it will not accept any dilution of the rights agreed to in that document, and prepared to take reciprocal action in the event Congress should block the treaty?
Further, should we decide on such action, do we have the means? That is where the great difficulty arises. It is the ineptness of the government over the past ten or 15 years which has brought us to this pass. I refer, of course, to the barely adequate enforcement machinery in the hands of the government in terms of accepting the responsibilities it assumed in extending Canadian jurisdiction. Government spokesmen maintain it is adequate. I maintain it is not.

The government contends we are talking about an international agreement, or a bi-national agreement, and that enforcement should be conducted by the flag state, that is, an offender would be judged in his own courts for an offence committed on the territory of the other state and that, in consequence, all that needs to be done is notify the flag state of an infraction, in the case of a foreign fisherman, leaving the imposition of sanctions to that state. In other words, a United States fisherman, even if he were caught in Canadian waters fishing illegally, would be brought to justice and penalized in the courts of the United States. A Canadian fisherman doing something wrong in American waters would be brought to justice by the Canadian courts.
It is extremely difficult, when one has completely inadequate enforcement machinery, to produce evidence in court to prove there has been an infraction of an agreement involving over-fishing or fishing in prohibited areas. To do so requires evidence taken on the spot by enforcers of agreements. I contend that the necessary measures should have been under construction during the past ten years when we knew we were headed for the 200-mile limit. All we do now is to notify the flag state that one of its ships is in breach of the agreement. We do this, presumably, on the evidence of overflights. But get the picture of a ship rocking on the waves somewhere out at sea! Mr. Speaker, I do not recall seeing the latitudes and longitudes marked on the waves. And that is what one has to prove.
Enforcement by the flag state is really no way of enforcing jurisdiction. And I don't want any smart cracks from the other side about us getting our act together, suggesting that fisheries spokesmen on this side are always talking about spending money while spokesmen for finance are always calling for restraint. I am talking about government policy over the past ten or 15 years. The government has done nothing during all that period. I could reel off on the fingers of my two hands the names of all the enforcement vessels on the west coast, and probably, using two hands and my feet, the number of tens of people there are to operate those boats. We hear that on one occasion when the salmon season was opening one ship was unable to sail because of engine trouble, another was in dry-dock, and a third could not find a crew to go out to sea. Those were the three coastguard vessels. When were they built? The first in service was built before some of the hon. members sitting in this chamber were born. It was built in 1932. Sure, she is up for auction at the moment. The most recent one was built in 1967, 11 years ago, and nothing I know of is going on the stocks.
Ten years ago our negotiating teams were in New York, Geneva, Venezuela, negotiating the Law of the Sea, knowing full well the time was coming when we would go to 200 miles. Still, nothing is on the stocks. There is nothing in the estimates, now, to provide for the vessels we need. I think it is scandalous.
Is it any wonder we are in trouble on the west coast? What about the Dixon entrance? Why cannot our negotiators secure something sensible and realistic? Why are we not taking every
May 11, 1978

step necessary to get Canadian rights off the Alaska panhandle to Canadian-bred fish breeding on their way back? Those are American waters, but do Canadian fishermen have any rights in those areas? No, because we cannot enforce those rights.
The parliamentary secretary knows what is happening. We are losing some fishing area there which we have claimed for a long time. We claim it, but we claim it with nothing to back up our claim. We do not back our fishermen up. We do not back our negotiators up, and it is high time there was something put into the estimates to back up our international negotiators and our fishermen.
The command structures we have are completely at sixes and sevens. They are not properly integrated. There are military, police, customs, fisheries, and research vessels out at sea at different times and in different places, but they do not have the power at all times to do fisheries patrol work. If they should find someone out of place, they do not have the power to use that as evidence. Not even out to the 50-mile limit do we have that.
It would surprise the House to learn that a commander of one of our service destroyers has to get special powers from the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) to stop a vessel. I think that is outrageous. He should have that warrant at all times. By contrast, at last count the U.S. coastguard-and I looked up some figures this morning which are about a year old-has 124 deep sea vessels, some with the capability of doing 29 knots. They have 36,300 men in their service, and there are 12,300 miles of coastline to patrol and defend. That 36,300 figure is just about half the size of our armed forces.
Where has this government put its priorities? We have 17,800 miles of coast line, and with the 200-mile limit we have increased our responsibilities over a third of our territory. What do we have by way of back-up to enforce our jurisdiction? We have nothing like what we need. Is it any wonder that we are in trouble when we are negotiating? We have had a very smart and good team negotiating at the Law of the Sea conference. I give that team full credit. We have a shrewd and capable negotiator dealing with the Americans. There is no question about that. We have made some yards on the international front in many areas, but on bilateral negotiations we have been going through with a whimper because we cannot back our negotiators up properly. Is there cause for concern? I think there is, unfortunately.
Fishing in British Columbia is an important industry which is worth defending. There are serious problems confronting the industry. Between 1976 and 1977 fish landings decreased on the Pacific coast by 19 per cent, about one fifth, from 383 million pounds to 322 million pounds. That was the Canadian catch. The Japanese, Russian, Polish and Korean landings were something else again. Prices were firm, and that is good. That is not the problem. Take-home pay was good, but poundage was bad. This could mean trouble in the years ahead, and
Fisheries
we have got to know somehow or other whether the problem is the result of foreign fishermen or declining stocks. These are important problems.
I now come to the question which was raised by my colleague, the hon. member for South Shore, when he talked about research. Yes, there has been some research. Much of it is going out by contract to individual private companies. That is fine, as long as there is no patronage, and one wonders.
I have here a document which indicates that $12 million worth of research has been going out to private companies in the last couple of years, more than $6 million a year. Some of that money went toward getting public reaction to the salmon enhancement program. There is no need to spend money learning public reaction. The salmon enhancement program is needed. The minister made a good case for it. Let us get on with it. Let us not spend money learning public reaction and putting out publicity. Let us get on with enhancing salmon stocks. That is what it is all about. This business about publicity, putting out brochures, having radio programs and so forth, is nonsense. It is all right for carrying on some of the work at international conferences. I would buy some of that, but I will not buy it to the extent it is revealed in this document.
Unfortunately there are more questions about fisheries than there are answers. Moreover, I am thinking only of the west coast. I have not touched on the Arctic or the east coast at all.
I have not touched on the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation in Manitoba or on the Great Lakes. The problems are immense. I dealt briefly with the west coast salmon problem and the need for additional policing and an international agreement.
What we obviously need is a reasonably just area assignment on the west coast under international agreements of some kind which will stick. We could call them international arrangements in order to avoid ratification. We could give them an umbrella treatment until a firm international agreement could be concluded and ratified in the appropriate manner in our two Houses. In these bilateral talks there are obviously trade-offs, extending fishing jurisdiction for Canadians to compensate for the fish take allowed to the Indians on the Olympic Peninsula and that sort of thing, but there is one other matter of great concern to me, and that is the effect on our fisheries of oil spills and the failure, again, of any coordinated approach to the whole matter. It has not proceeded far enough. There have been some talks, but the government has been delinquent in this area, as in all the others.
The government has known for years that oil tankers would be coming down our Pacific coast from Valdez. I am informed that the location of clean-up equipment is all on a computer. I am going to get a print-out. I have yet to see a print-out.

I will try to summarize quickly because I know other speakers want the floor. There is the matter of compensation. Under American law there is provision for some $200 million as a compensation fund. Under Canadian law there is provision for a $40 million compensation fund, one fifth that of the American fund. That is not enough. We have more coast. More damage can be done to our coast than to the U.S. coast.
Then there is the matter of liability and traffic controls. The traffic controls, they say, are now voluntary and they may be mandatory in due course. What about the standards of shipbuilding, the standards of seaworthiness, crewing standards and the placement of the clean-up equipment? I contend that all this deserves a place in a bilateral agreement between Canada and the United States. I am referring to compensation, liability, mandatory traffic controls, shipbuilding standards, crewing standards and all related matters affecting the pollution and the deterioration of the breeding and migratory grounds of our fish. All these deserve a place in a bilateral agreement to which Canada and the United States should be bound.
There are other areas with which I would like to deal but I cannot do so now. I shall leave to someone else the salmon enhancement program. For all the reasons I have stated, because of the government's shortcomings, its lack of foresight and its inadequacy, I subscribe fully to every word of the motion put forward by the hon. member for South Shore, and I enjoin others to do likewise.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the Leader of Opposition (Mr. Clark) is present because the previous speaker, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), took a great deal of time suggesting that the federal government is not enforcing the 200-mile limit and that we should spend literally millions of dollars on the purchase of vessels. I would like to take a few minutes to comment on what the hon. member has said, because I think that if we look very closely at what has happened in the first year of enforcement of our 200-mile zone, we will find that the first interesting thing was that before 1977 Canada had negotiated with the distant water fishing fleets and had signed agreements with 90 per cent of those fleets that they would respect the 200-mile limit.

speechtext: Oh, come on!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
Obviously the hon. member does not like hearing the truth. By obtaining agreements with these distant water fishing fleets, we saved Canada innumerable millions of dollars. On the question of inspections, instead of having very expensive ships or aircraft patrolling the world's largest coastline, what we have done in many cases where a distant water fishing fleet had obtained a licence from the Canadian government is to send one fisheries officer by helicopter to the mother ship. The fisheries officer went on board the ship and stayed there during the whole time that the ship was in Canadian waters. I am sorry the hon. member has left the chamber. What we have done is to save millions and millions of dollars by having someone on board the distant water fishing fleets. We had only one man doing the job instead of a ship worth several millions of dollars crewed by thirty or forty people.
The hon. member is proposing that we should spend literally hundreds of millions of dollars when we can hire fisheries officers to go out on-board these ships, and thus gain much better knowledge of what is being fished, how much is being fished and what type of species is being fished. Because obviously that gentleman on board the ship sees the fish coming on board. I hope the Leader of the Opposition will have a good talk with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and will tell him that it is in the interests of Canadian fishermen not to throw money down the drain but to use our resources in a logical manner.
Perhaps the hon. member is not aware of the fact that in 1977 fourteen convictions were recorded against foreign captains for breaking Canadian regulations. Also, our fisheries people have issued warnings and cancellations of licences. I understand that on the east coast alone, 900 foreign fishing vessels were inspected by the Department of Fisheries and also 170 Canadian fishing boats.
So I caution those who would literally spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a process that we do not require. I hope that the licensing system we have instigated whereby foreign nations must apply to Canada for a licence, following which we allow them to enter at a point of entry, specify the length of stay and the amount of catch and have one fisheries officer on board, makes much more sense than the suggestion put forward by the hon. member earlier.
Let us consider the motion before us today. I think its allegations can be refuted in several ways. First of all, I should like to quote the minister of fisheries for British Columbia, the Hon. Rafe Main, who spoke at the federal-provincial conference which was recently held in Ottawa. He spoke on the subject of fisheries, and after making his initial comments on behalf of British Columbia, he said the following:
In summary, Mr. Prime Minister, we are very pleased with the co-operation that we have with the federal government... We have had hitherto, Mr. Prime Minister, this co-operation in British Columbia and we sincerely hope it will continue and British Columbia hopes to make it continue.
May 11, 1978

That is slightly different from what the motion says, that co-operation with the provincial ministers does not exist. Lack of consultation was also alleged. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) has tabled several documents regarding meetings he has had with premiers and with fishing groups, but he did not say much about them-he is a very modest man. Let me give the timetable of the minister for the current month, specifying his meetings with provincial ministers and with fishing groups. For example, tomorrow the minister will be meeting with the B.C. Wildlife Federation in Abbottsford, B.C. On May 5 the minister met with R. Cashin, president of Newfoundland Fishermen, Food and Allied Workers. On May 5 he met in Halifax with Premier Regan of Nova Scotia. On the same day in Halifax with Premier Regan and the Hon. Dan Reid. Again on the same day he met in Halifax with the Hon. F. Mooney. On the same day in Halifax he met with the Digby scallopers. On May 3 in Quebec City the minister met with the Fisheries Council of Canada. On May 2 in Ottawa he met with Richard Cashin, president of Newfoundland Fishermen, Food and Allied Workers. That was his timetable in May. These have been the activities of the minister in meeting with interested groups, fishermen and ministers.
On April 17 the minister met in Winnipeg with the provincial ministers responsible for fisheries for the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Ontario and the Northwest Territories. On the same day in Winnipeg he had a meeting with Kip Thompson and other representatives of northern Manitoba fishermen. On April 10 in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, the minister met with Don Cadegan, president of Highland Fisheries. On the same day in Cape Breton he met with Arthur LeBlanc, president of the United Maritime Fishermen. Again on the same day in Cape Breton he met with representatives of the processors of Richmond Fisheries, Isle Madame Fishermen's Co-op, the Louisbourg division of National Sea Products, Peter Mullen's Limited, H. Hopkins Limited in Louisbourg and the Highland Fisheries Limited of Glace Bay. I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. I have several pages of this timetable which the minister has already tabled.
This motion alleges lack of consultation. What I have done is to describe the minister's activities during an approximate 30-day period. The minister has already said that holding meetings does not necessarily mean that an agreement is achieved. However, this motion condemns the minister for his lack of consultation with the provinces and with Fisheries groups. ! think that the material that he has tabled today refutes that charge.
Comments were made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) regarding the problems we have had with the implementation of the 200-mile limit and with the injunction taken out in the United States. I agree that the hon. member is quite correct when he indicates that we have had problems.
a (1742)
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich brought up the point that we do not patrol our 200-mile limit. Perhaps we
Fisheries
should take a look at what happened in Canada with the 200-mile limit, as well as what has happened in other countries as they have implemented 200-mile limits. Perhaps it would be useful to compare the experiences in other parts of the world, developments in fisheries management in other 200-mile zones of jurisdiction, with the Canadian experience. A number of examples come to mind in various parts of the world where the movement is toward centralization and the development of larger units to deal with fisheries questions.
The European Economic Community is continuing to develop a common fisheries policy to deal with questions in areas such as the North Sea, where the zones of a number of the member states and non-member states border on each other, and where serious conservation problems have developed in the free-for-all which existed before the community's extension of jurisdiction to 200 miles. Now the EEC acts as spokesman for its member states in fisheries matters when dealing with other European countries and foreign nations abroad.
This is not to say the problems which existed before the implementation of the 200-mile limit have been solved. However, the EEC is establishing or attempting to establish a common fisheries policy. Anyone who reads the European press will be aware of the questions involving the proposed exclusive fishing zones for Britain and Ireland. Despite these internal problems, however, it is true to say that the European Economic Community is moving toward a centralized system of fisheries.
In the Antipodes, a large number of South Pacific island states including Australia and New Zealand are working toward a system of central management of fisheries resources in an area which encompasses many thousands of square miles of ocean. In West Africa there are problems in fisheries management due to the very narrow strips of water that have been created by the 200-mile limit. In Latin America, particularly on the Pacific coast, the Latin American states recognize their common interest.
One of the few examples of where a centralization of fisheries has not taken place is within the United States. Prior to the United States extension of fisheries jurisdiction on March 1, 1977, the individual coastal states enjoyed control over fisheries resources out to three miles from shore, with the federal government having control in the contiguous zone from 3 to 12 miles.
In the United States, extension of fisheries jurisdiction to 200 miles was accomplished through the initiative of congress, which in 1976 passed the fisheries conservation and management act that was to take effect on March 1, 1977. This legislation placed the prime responsibility for ocean fisheries management in the hands of eight regional fisheries management councils. The councils' mandate was to review all aspects of fisheries management, including regulations, total allowable catches, United States harvesting capacity, and surpluses available to foreign nations.
The membership of the regional councils is determined by the United States Secretary of Commerce. In the make-up of the councils, there is substantial input ranging from a reliance
5338

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
in some cases on academics and professional fisheries managers to relying in other cases on substantial input from the fishing industry.
Each regional council has a great deal of independence. This independence has caused some of the problems which were mentioned by the hon. member in his earlier remarks. This independence has caused a problem not only in American waters, but also in dealing with other countries. These difficulties flow from the fact that while the Secretary of Commerce must make determinations on fisheries management matters based on regional council recommendations, it is the Secretary of State who is charged with the negotiation of bilateral agreements. Sometimes we think we have created a bureaucratic nightmare. Can one imagine the bureaucratic nightmare which exists in the United States today in fisheries management?
I would dare to suggest the flexibility of the United States is severely limited by the determinations made by the Secretary of Commerce. This has created significant problems for Canada. These problems arise not only from the fact that regional councils are charged with defending local rather than national interests, but also from the fact that United States legislation did not provide for any special relationship with its two closest neighbours, namely, Canada and Mexico.
Therefore, the United States is experiencing a fragmentation of fisheries management. There is no guarantee the regional councils will carry out the policies of the national government in respect of fisheries. The current problems being experienced between Canada and the United States are indicative of this phenomenon. Both countries have attempted to develop rational management measures for fish stocks of mutual interest.
Ambassador Cadieux for Canada and Ambassador Cutler for the United States were appointed and instructed to report to both governments by October 1977 on the principles of a comprehensive settlement, and to develop the substance of an ad referendum agreement for submission to both governments, if possible, by the end of 1977. The two special negotiators succeeded in agreeing on a set of principles encompassing fisheries and hydro-carbon resource arrangements, and an interim joint report was submitted to the governments on October 14, 1977. In the next phase, efforts were directed at securing agreement on precise boundary lines, the exact terms of an over-all bilateral fisheries agreement, and the institutionalization of a system for shared access to hydro-carbons in the boundary areas.
Since October 1977, the negotiators, their officials and advisers have met regularly in both countries. In fact, negotiations are taking place in Ottawa today between Mr. Cadieux and Mr. Cutler. They have consulted closely with their respective provincial state and industry interests. It should be brought out at this time that in these negotiations representatives from the fishing industry processors, UFAWU, trawlers, et cetera, have been a part of the Canadian negotiating team.
I think the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands asked that specific question of the minister. He

referred to the participation of Canadians in the negotiations. Canadians have been very much involved. I can report that they have met on numerous occasions to discuss the Canadian position. Their input is welcome, as their input was welcome at the Law of the Sea conference where Canada had the largest delegation of any nation. Canada's delegation consisted of government experts, experts from the industry and the unions, as well as native fishermen from British Columbia and the Pacific trawlers. In order to have an expert team, we believe the input of those people who are most closely associated with the industry is required.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion, of course, is one where we condemn-
-the federal Minister of Fisheries for his failure to consult and co-operate with provincial fisheries ministers and fishermen prior to establishing arbitrary rules and regulations which are harmful to the fishermen, and for his failure to develop a positive policy for the protection and development of the Canadian fishing industry in order to derive maximum advantage for Canadians from the extended jurisdiction.
Let me say at the start that I have a lot of admiration for our Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc). I think that of the Liberal ministers of fisheries the present occupant of that post is the best that we have had from that party. I was the minister of fisheries in Newfoundland in 1974 when he was the minister here. The fishing industry had hit rock bottom and it was a question of whether or not it was going to survive. Because of
Fisheries
the minister's policies and other factors, and because of the work that was done in Newfoundland and other provinces, we have come out of that and the fisheries are now on the way up.
The trouble with the minister is that he now thinks he has all the answers. Unfortunately, he has become extremely arbitrary, extremely dictatorial and guaranteed to ruffle the feathers-if not the feathers, the scales-of any provincial minister of fisheries. It is not only of Newfoundland that I speak, it is of the four Atlantic provinces in particular. I do not know how he relates to British Columbia. It is not only a question of politics. The Newfoundland government is a PC government, in New Brunswick it is PC, in P.E.I. it is Liberal, and in Nova Scotia it is Liberal-but it will not be much longer. But even in a province like Nova Scotia we find the premier of that province saying on April 19 in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald'.
The Canadian constitution should be reformed to give the provinces more jurisdiction over fisheries, Premier Gerald Regan said during question period in the legislature yesterday ...
Outside the House, fisheries minister Dan Reid said this is a change all four Atlantic provinces are advocating.
"The whole direction of the fishery and how it affects the province and its economy now rests on the whims of Ottawa."
This is what a Liberal minister said:
He said many problems are created by this lack of control. "We are closer to the scene here and could deal with them more appropriately."
These are Liberal premiers and ministers, Mr. Speaker, saying this because what the federal minister is forgetting is that the fishery is life and death in the Atlantic provinces. Or at least, it is life and death to Newfoundland.
It may be that the fishery contribution to the gross national product is under one per cent, Mr. Speaker, but to Newfoundland it is tremendous. At least 20,000 people are directly employed as fishermen or fish processors out of a work force altogether of some 180,000 people. The indirect and direct employment effect on Newfoundland is gigantic, plus the fact that in three-quarters of the province you cannot live in the communities that are now settled there without a viable fishery. Therefore, we feel, and rightly so, that it must have more say over the fishery.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we went for supper I was describing how important the fishery was to Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces, why we resent so much the arrogant attitude of the Minister of Fisheries and why, if this is not

changed and corrected, there is going to be a major confrontation between Newfoundland and the Government of Canada. I pointed out that in Nova Scotia even the Liberal premier and a Liberal minister were very chagrined, disappointed and angry at the relationship.
I have one final quotation from a Halifax newspaper of April 26, where again the fisheries minister of Nova Scotia, Dr. Reid, said:
The federal fisheries department has not honoured its pledge to seek more consultation and co-operation with the provincial fisheries department and local fishermen.
In an interview he went on to say that, despite assurances of closer co-operation during the recent first ministers' conference, the province still has no say in many of the sweeping federal regulations handed down.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in the last ten years in Newfoundland we have got a real department of fisheries. We have a minister of fisheries that knows his stuff. We have a good deputy minister of fisheries and we have a good department. The years of Smallwood neglect are over. They're not dumb-bells, they're not yo-yos, they're not yokels; they're not dumb, ignorant Newfoundlanders who have to do whatever some minister up here in Ottawa tells them. We are sick down there of being treated like that. Not only that, but when it comes to spending the money on the fishery there is considerably more being spent in proportion by the Newfoundland government than is being spent by the Ottawa bureaucrats.
If we just look at the one area of construction of vessels and assistance given for the construction of vessels, last year in Newfoundland the provincial government made $9.2 million available in assistance to fishermen to buy and construct new vessels by way of loans and subsidies. The federal government, this great federal government in Ottawa, spent exactly $600,000 for those purposes in Newfoundland.
In Newfoundland they are also putting their money where their mouths are. They want to be consulted and involved in the fishery. We want to be consulted and involved in the future of our province. We have seen industrial development after industrial development fail. We have seen the fishery come back so that it is going to mean something in our future. We are not satisfied to have the Minister of Fisheries, no matter how good he might be here in Ottawa, deciding the life and death of our province by himself. We are not satisfied. We are not going to put up with it. We are not going to tolerate it. What does the Newfoundland minister of fisheries say about how they have been treated? I quote from the May 9 Daily News:
"We should be given a greater responsibility in the control of our fishery ... right now we are seldom even consulted concerning policy ... I am not content to let a bunch of Upper Canadian bureaucrats dictate how we in Newfoundland should control our resource ..
That was said by the minister of fisheries in Newfoundland. The premier of Newfoundland said the same. In the Evening

Telegram of May 6 the minister of fisheries is quoted as having said:
The Newfoundland government is going to "fight like hell" and take legal action, if necessary, to prove it has a right to have a voice in the management of the fishery resources off the coast of the province.
I do not blame the Newfoundland minister of fisheries. He has been treated abominably, as has been the case with the minister from Nova Scotia. In May of last year our minister of fisheries, Mr. Carter, put a proposal to the federal fisheries people about fisheries development in Newfoundland. In May he had proposals for the landing of additional fish for processing in seasonal plants, how to acquire additional ships and co-operative fishing ventures with the Portuguese, upgrading and expanding the fleet and so on. He was advised by Ottawa in September, I think, that Newfoundland's plan would not be considered on its own merit, but rather it would be considered only in the Atlantic provinces context. In other words, Newfoundland would be permitted by Ottawa to proceed in matters of fisheries development only as it related to and at a pace with the other Atlantic provinces. Is it any wonder they have gone berserk in Newfoundland?
The fishery means more to Newfoundland than any other province and they have been told they have to go along at the snail's pace that some other province might want to go. Proposals of Newfoundland are treated with contempt. Our ministers are treated as though they were office boys and busboys by the federal minister. No wonder the relationship between the minister and his provincial counterparts are exacerbated.
On December 1, 1977, the four Atlantic provinces put in a proposal to the Minister of Fisheries with the collective views of the four provinces. We know there are four disadvantaged provinces, four suppliant provinces, provinces that get the fiscal Kung Fu foot right in the face if they dare raise their voices and do not do what they are told by great Uncle Ottawa. The four provinces put in a proposal on what should happen in fisheries development. It has been treated with scorn, derision and contempt by the Minister of Fisheries as though they are not to be listened to. One of their proposals was that $910 million should be spent over the next ten years to replace the present fishing fleet, $260 million to replace half the inshore fleet because it is becoming obsolete, $500 million to replace half the offshore wetfish trawler fleet, and $150 million for new vessels to start replacing the foreign fishing effort. That is the proposal.
The Minister of Fisheries treats them and their proposal as though it were a case of leprosy, that if this proposal were touched, his hand would fall off, or his fins would fall off, or his tail would fall off. He thinks this is a terrible proposal that these four provinces put in. The minister infers they should be locked up, that they are criminal for what they want to do in expanding the Canadian fishing fleet. The minister says they have to be more conservative, more careful.
The Newfoundland government does not see why the federal minister should refuse to license additional Canadian-controlled vessels to fish in the 200-mile limit while foreign
May 11, 1978

nations are given licences to fish there. There are 500 foreign fishing vessels that have been given licences to fish within our 200-mile limit and the minister says Canadians are not to have additional licences to fish. He pooh-poohs, scoffs, scorns and attacks proposals of the four Atlantic provinces for starting to make preparations to replace existing obsolete trawlers on a ten-year program at $91 million a year.
It is time the members of the fisheries committee or some other appropriate committee had a good look at future policy in the fishery because we are headed on a collision course. I admire the minister for many of the things he has done, as I said earlier before six o'clock. However, he is too stiff-necked, too arrogant and too convinced that he and he alone has the answer. He forgets the fishery is life and death to Newfoundland. We are not going to have our life or death decided by Romeo LeBlanc or any federal politician.

speechtext:
I am not supposed to use his name; 1 mean the Minister of Fisheries. We are not going to let one man control our destiny and future like that.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) put on a charade at the February first ministers' conference and pretended that the provinces would be more involved in these decisions. When I questioned the minister in the fisheries committee a few weeks later, he smiled knowingly as he indicated that nothing was going to be done to follow up that pious protestation of the Prime Minister.
We are upset. This is life and death to Newfoundland. In my own district, one third of the voters live in the rural area. Our rural area depends on the fishery. I am not satisfied to have the Minister of Fisheries of Canada decide on the life and death of the various communities in my constituency.
I wish I had time to give all their names. I could start at Come-By-Chance where the oil refinery used to operate. There is now nothing but the fishery there. Every community in our rural area is dependent on the fishery. In St. John's we have a major fish plant. St. John's itself depends on the fishery. It depends on the rest of the island for its livelihood as a distributing centre and the rest of it. That is why they are so exercised in Newfoundland.
If occasionally someone on the mainland hears of some discontent from the Newfoundland government, they should understand why it is. If the future of Ontario was being decided by one cabinet minister here and he would not listen to the provincial government, you can be assured that the papers would be full of it. We would hear of nothing else. It would rage on for weeks. It would be in the Globe and Mail on the first page, the second page and the editorial page. It would be in the Toronto Star, the Toronto this and the Toronto that. That is all we would hear about in the rest of Canada if that were the case.
One man has determined the destiny of Newfoundland. They are told to keep their mouths shut in Newfoundland as
Fisheries
though they are ignorant cuffs that should not be heard. We are certainly not noticed in the mainland press.
If the Minister of Fisheries is to be a successful minister, he will have to change his ways. The fisheries committee will need to have a look at the future of fisheries development. There is much to talk about, but we never have enough time to do it. If I were allowed to occupy the time between now and 10:30, I could maybe deal with it half adequately.
We have a longiiner fleet in Newfoundland. The Minister of Fisheries says there is no need to replace any of those longlin-ers. There used to be a 35 per cent federal subsidy on longiiner construction of vessels in Newfoundland. The minister has cut it out. The Newfoundland government has gone ahead with the building of 20 longliners from 55 feet to 65 feet. Today it costs $250,000 for a 55-foot vessel and $350,000 to $400,000 for a 65-foot vessel.
The Minister of Fisheries cut out the 35 per cent federal subsidy. The province is paying a 15 per cent subsidy and is giving loans for 95 per cent at 3 per cent interest. If the federal government does not come through, the poor province of Newfoundland has to put up the other 35 per cent to get these boats in the hands of the fishery.
The Minister of Fisheries says that more longliners are not needed. The government last year was abused by the Minister of Fisheries of Canada for having the audacity and daring to build a longiiner on its own. There were 120 applications for those 20 longliners, 60 of which were found to be qualified. Only 20 of that 60 will be able to get a boat. What is the federal government going to do? The minister suggested in his recent speech to the Fisheries Council of Canada on May 3, 1978, that he is going to cut out the subsidies that they used to pay on boats. He said at page 16 of his address:
Will Atlantic fishing be profitable enough so that, as in B.C., we can do away with all boat-building subsidies?
He has already done away with them. He is just flying a balloon there. The Newfoundland trawler fleet needs replacements over the next ten years. The minister is doing nothing but pooh-poohing the idea. A solemn commitment was made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) in connection with the Cape Sambro. There is still owing $930,000 in federal payments. The minister has to get around that and get it paid or the commitment by the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be broken.
What is wrong with the federal bureaucracy? In my district of Arnold's Cove, there is a proposal from National Sea Products Limited. They want a million dollars in loans from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. They want the ordinary DREE assistance for job creation to expand their fish plant in Arnold's Cove. They are going to take the herring and process it to the final finished product so that we will not be shipping it out in bulk to Norway and buying it back in little bottles with little bits of herring in them for 50 times the price.

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
This was the most successful proposal ever made to DREE. DREE complains that it cannot get enough proposals for private enterprise in Newfoundland and that is why they are so low in the payments they make under their program. Yet that proposal has been in since October and three or four weeks ago I received a silly reply from the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) saying that he doesn't yet know whether the fishery resource can stand the expansion of this plant which is going to create 67 new jobs at Arnold's Cove in the Come-By-Chance area where the unemployment rate, I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, is about 50 per cent.
I ask the Minister of Fisheries to give the minister for DREE a boot right where he ought to be booted and get that proposal out. Get this extension to the fish plant going at Arnold's Cove in Newfoundland. The hon. gentleman is closer to the Minister for DREE than I am or I would give him the boot myself. I have to use sweetness and light because I am in the opposition; I cannot use the harsh tactics I would otherwise use to expose this bureaucratic nonsense-that it takes five or six months to approve a proposal like this when money is lashed out by DREE in every direction in other provinces.
The German firm, Nordsee, Mr. Speaker, made a proposal to the FIRB-the Foreign Investment Review Board-at the beginning of December, 1977 to take over a 51 per cent interest in Ocean Harvesters Limited in Harbour Grace, and it has not been dealt with yet. No decision has been made five months later. The Minister of Fisheries says he is opposed to it. He is so rude, he is so ignorant in connection with the proposal, that he refuses even to see the Nordsee company or its representatives. He says he is not going to have any foreign capital investment in the fishery.
Well, this is a new departure, Mr. Speaker. The minister had better look at the figures and see how capital is flying out of Canada before he starts preventing foreign capital from coming in to our fishing industry. The minister makes vague statements such as this-I quote from his speech of May 3:
Foreign capital investment need not and should not become a major feature of the Canadian fishing industry on the east coast or on the west.
Note the word "major". Who is arguing that it should be major? Here is a German firm that has the marketing expertise, one of the largest fishing companies in the world. It wants to invest in this plant in Harbour Grace and put five trawlers there. It will give year-round employment there and put the plant on its feet in an area of heavy unemployment in Newfoundland. Yet because of some ideological reason the Minister of Fisheries says he won't give them a licence for their trawlers. Who does he think he is? Does he think he is God? Does he think these hundreds of people in Harbour Grace should be denied year-round livelihood because of some ideological reason the minister does not even explain properly? He is not going to let our zone be taken over by the back door, he says, by foreign companies borrowing our flag to catch our fish. They don't need to borrow our flag to catch the fish. There are 500 of them with licences now. What utter tripe and nonsense, Mr. Speaker. "I do not want so see the Maple Leaf become the world's fishing flag", the minister says. What has

that to do with it? I say the minister should finish this up. His deskmate just up the row here had a different attitude. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) said, and I quote from the Globe and Mail of March 25:
Trade and Commerce Minister Jack Horner has said that the Newfoundland Government has a "pretty compelling case" and indicated that the Foreign Investment Review Agency, which is now considering the application, should look favourably on it.
That's what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said, while the Minister of Fisheries says he has refused to give them a licence. The Newfoundland government now has a deal in which it has said that, in addition to many other safeguarding conditions, it is going to take a 6 per cent interest so that the German company cannot control Ocean Harvesters Limited. It will be controlled by Canadians. And yet we still have this stubborn attitude by the Minister of Fisheries, who does not explain very clearly why this proposal is to be prevented at all costs. You wonder that we are puzzled down in Newfoundland by all these peculiar things which are happening.
We are also puzzled in my district, in Bay Bulls, as to why a $3 million centre has not been started yet. In the December 5, 1977 Daily News the regional director of fisheries said the new multi-million-dollar marine service centre was going to be under construction early in 1978. They were going to station their fisheries vessels there. However, he is now saying that the planning is going ahead, that there should be some evidence of work on that facility before the end of 1978. Well, the evidence is not strong enough, Mr. Speaker. There is a dirty suspicion that it is not going ahead as quickly as it was. I won the by-election in 1976, and the people of Bay Bulls and I don't like it. I want that job under way very shortly, Mr. Speaker. Never mind the planning. I want the proof. I want them to carry out the plans that were announced for Bay Bulls.
The province seeks permission to lease freezer ships. The province has to ask the permission of the Minister of Fisheries of Canada to do anything you can think of, Mr. Speaker. In order to overcome the glut problem during peak periods in the cod fishery, the Newfoundland government wants to lease some freezer ships to help take the surplus fish. They haven't got an answer yet from the Minister of Fisheries.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will have to cool it. Now, I do not wish to be unfair to the Minister of Fisheries. Quite seriously, I said I think he is the best Liberal Minister of Fisheries we have had since 1949. He has done many good things for the fishery. But, Mr. Speaker, he is on the verge of spoiling that very fine record with his attitude toward Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces, for the very reasons I have described here. It is life and death to us and we are not going to leave our life or our death in the fishery in the hands of one minister in Ottawa. He has got to share his authority and his power. He has got to start a process of real consulta-
May 11, 1978

tion. He has got to show less arrogance. He has got to start listening to the provincial ministers. They are not dumb-dumbs or dodos. They have something to say and we have good departments of fisheries in our provinces-all four of them. We can see the old dreams of industrial glory are gone. They have gone down, and everybody has come back to the realization that it was the fishery which originally caused the settlement of Newfoundland, that it is what will save Newfoundland, if it is to be saved, as well as the offshore minerals which we trust will come in over the next 10 or 15 years.
This is why the minister has to learn to change his attitude, and it is why I suggest that the House of Commons fisheries committee should spend a couple of weeks with the minister and his officials, and with the provincial minister and his officials, and have a good look at the future policies of our fisheries and see if we can agree. Let us let it all hang out and get some of these problems solved, and get the fishery on a proper basis with real co-operation between the five governments.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this special debate with pride and enthusiasm but also with some frustration and regret. I rise with pride because I come from a fishing industry family, because I know and respect and have fought for the needs of the fishing industry, and because I belong to a government which has done more for Canada's fishermen in the last four years than has been done in any previous period in our history.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
Extension of the fishery limit to 200 miles has added impetus to upgraded search and rescue capability and a $350 million enhancement program designed to double our catch of salmonoid species on the Pacific coast. Perhaps most important, a strong and informed and concerned Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) has been an effective advocate for all fishermen in this country. All these things have combined in recent years, Mr. Speaker, to make the prospects for the fishing industry look exceedingly bright for fishermen from Newfoundland to the Queen Charlotte Islands and from Yarmouth to Kincolith.
I also rise in frustration and regret, Mr. Speaker, because it is very clear that the real and serious problems which do exist in the fishing industry and in the relations of our country with the United States have been blown entirely out of proportion by those with a vested interest in sensationalism and in division. In the face of the undeniable proof of this government's understanding of the needs of the fishing industry and its remarkable commitment to meeting those needs, there are still some who say that we do not understand and that we are actively seeking to sell out to the Americans. This is not good logic. In fact this is not logic at all. I think I need only remind the House of our tough, reasoned approach in the current marine boundary and fish management negotiations and of the extensive consultations among the federal government, provincial governments and representatives of the fishing industry to put those silly conclusions that follow from such logic to rest.
Fisheries
I would like to deal with the aspects of the current marine boundaries negotiations which are of particular relevance to the Pacific coast, especially to the halibut fishery. But I want first of all to respond directly to the Conservative motion suggesting that there has been inadequate consultation between our negotiators and representatives of the fishing industry.
In less than a year there have been six plenary sessions of the joint U.S.-Canada boundary negotiations attended by so many industry and provincial representatives that one special observer I spoke to, sir, referred to it as a mini-United Nations. The groups from British Columbia which attended these successful sessions included the following: the Fisheries Association of British Columbia, representing many fish processors in the province, the Pacific Trailers' Association, the Pacific Gillnetters' Association, the Central Native Cooperative, representing the native people who have made the Bella Bella Cannery successful, the Native Brotherhood of B.C., the Prince Rupert Fishermen's Co-operative, The United Fishermen's and Allied Workers' Union; the Co-operative Fishermen's Guild, the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs, the Nishga Tribal Council, The Association of B.C. Independent Fishermen, and the Fishing Vessel Owners of B.C.
In addition to the six plenary sessions, each of these groups has had the opportunity to participate in smaller sessions dealing with specific aspects of the fisheries agreement, those dealing with particular fish stocks or particular geographical areas.
When certain representatives were unable to attend sessions because of commitments elsewhere-for instance, if they were out fishing-the consultative process was held for them so that they could join with the negotiators. These special arrangements were made many times. Our ambassador, Mr. Cadieux, has done so personally at least three times to my knowledge, and his closest assistants have done exactly the same thing. It was only on April 20 that a party of four negotiating members of the team came to a public meeting in Prince Rupert organized by the Prince Rupert Labour Council and consulted at length.
In addition to industry consultations the federal negotiators have met frequently in many types of forums with representatives of the marine resources branch of the B.C. department of recreation and conservation. To imply that these people do not know how to negotiate I really believe is a shocking suggestion for the opposition to make. Speaking of that consultation, I have here three enormous pieces of paper-

Mr. Speaker, I do not believe we have to have sexist interruptions from the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).
During these sessions the participants know that important work is being done. I would also like to point out for hon. members opposite that the salmonoid enhancement program is one which will benefit all west coasters. There are regulations to be thought of with regard to the Indian food fishery, which is a very high priority of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. Another priority is to ensure the safety of vessels during particularly difficult fisheries, such as the herring roe fishery just completed. Involved in these meetings were 17 private organizations and at least five provincial ministries.
Since the beginning of this year, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has had 14 separate meetings with industry representatives on the west coast. This record of briefing and consultation speaks for itself. The minister, his officials and the special negotiators charged with the difficult task of charting new marine boundaries and of ensuring the proper joint management of fish resources have been thorough in their efforts to consult the people they represent.
As always, there are those who apparently feel that they stand to gain politically or otherwise by spreading the patent lie that the Canadian government is selling out the interests of its citizens, and there are those who apparently delight in creating division and disunity for motives which are unclear to responsible Canadians.
I hope, now that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has put to rest the concerns of the opposition as to whether there will be an election-

speechtext: He hasn't the courage.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)

speechtext:
-those delighters in division will take off their cloaks of hypocrisy and help us deal in a positive and constructive manner with the real problems we face.
We face a number of problems with respect to Canadian-American fishing relations, and we face them because certain elements of the American fishing industry are clearly trying to subvert the intent of the 1978 interim fisheries agreement reached between our two countries, an agreement which provides for compensation for Canadian fishermen who suffered losses as a result of the failure of the Americans to live up to the terms of the 1977 interim agreement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: You can make a good speech; why do you want to read?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman opposite should take note of the fact that his friend, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), said that we must remember that sweetness and light are the watchwords for all oppositionists.
In any event, I want to go back to the interim agreement. Certainly it was an unfortunate situation in 1977 and, if actions rather than threats are taken in violation of the interim agreement, then Canadian fishing interests will suffer. Cer-

tainly the interests of our fishermen must be protected. This government will protect them, as any responsible observer will agree that it has been doing all along. But is shrill rhetoric and painting images of sell-out and the threatening of a fish war the most responsible and productive way to go about resolving the situation? Nobody wins in a fish war, least of all the fish, on which the future earnings of all fishermen depend. The issue is too important and too complex for the simple slogans and scare stories that some parties seem to prefer to consultation and advice.
As an example of the complexities involved I wish briefly to discuss the problems faced by just one of the fisheries which may be affected by American failure to honour the interim agreement. The 1978 halibut fishing season opens next Monday, May 15, and already the boats have set out from Prince Rupert to the waters off the Alaska panhandle and into Dixon Entrance. It is a small but important fishery off Alaska, with 30 to 40 vessels and some 300 fishermen taking part. It is both historic and important to the north, and it is an international fishery. In the coming year Canadian fishermen are expected to land halibut from Alaskan waters worth approximately $4.7 million. American fishermen could land halibut from Canadian waters worth about $700,000. In other words, the potential loss to Canadian fishermen this year, if they were denied access to the U.S. zone, would be in the amount of approximately $4 million.
Clearly, those who speak eagerly about a fish war are not doing so with the best interests of our halibut fishermen in mind. If, indeed, worse should come to worst and we should decide that we must terminate the interim fisheries agreement because of American failure to abide by its terms, then our halibut fishermen would be among the first, and unfortunately, the worst, losers. They would have to be-and I am assured that they would be-compensated by our government for their losses, but surely they would prefer and surely we would all prefer that they be out on the fishing waters they have traditionally fished.
The elements of the current interim agreement which some U.S. fishermen insist on ignoring-causing us to retaliate-are those relating to protection and management of our own fishery. The need for conservation is clearly evidenced by the need to increase the take of valuable protein from the sea and to provide employment for a strong fisheries industry on the west coast.
As fish have the annoying habit of swimming from the territorial waters of one country to those of another, and as fishermen apparently have trouble, on occasion, charting exactly where an ocean boundary is when the line is on the map and not on the water, it is clearly understood that international agreements are needed to protect this resource, and we must have the assurance that individual fishermen will live up to those agreements. We do not want to be without an
May 11, 1978

agreement with the Americans, but an agreement which is not interpreted in the same way by both sides may be worse than none at all. Our course is clear. We want to have an agreement. The fisheries resource needs the protection of a universally accepted agreement. The fact that we are not prepared to sign an agreement which does not offer these assurances is ample proof that no sell-out has ever been considered nor, indeed, ever will be.
There is one more aspect of the halibut fishery to which I would like to return for a moment, and that is the question of the A-B line, the Dixon Entrance portion of the boundary between Canada and the Alaska panhandle. The halibut fishery takes place in Dixon Entrance in waters on both sides of the A-B line. There is legitimate concern on the part of Canadian fishermen that American officials may act on the American position that the A-B line is a disputed boundary and seize Canadian vessels within three miles of that line.
While I do not expect this to happen, especially if cooler heads prevail and inflammatory statements and actions are subdued, I know our government is aware of the situation, is monitoring it very closely, and is prepared to offer full assistance to any Canadian vessel should it be illegally detained by American authorities.
What concerns me more than this, however, are the ill-founded and potentially dangerous rumours being circulated by those who either should know better or perhaps feel they stand to gain in some mysterious way by being irresponsible. Perhaps their gain will be political. The rumours indicate that Canada has acceded to American demands to shift the A-B line south. In the clearest possible language, such reports are not true. The only possible reason for movement of the A-B line would be if the Americans offered us something better, an irresistible offer of something better for Canadian fishermen in return. They have not done this, and consequently we have made no agreement to move the A-B line. The likelihood is slim indeed that we ever will.
I am concerned about this because among the people spreading such patently false rumours is one person who has acted as an adviser to the Canadian negotiating team, one who has been the recipient of confidential briefing information and who is aware of what the Canadian position is. This person is a regular guest on CBC news and knows full well that no agreement has been made to move the A-B line. Yet for whatever misplaced reason, this person continues to foster this myth, along with others of clearer political motivation. That can only weaken the position of our negotiating team.
This motion is about consultation and the alleged lack of consultation by the government with parties concerned about the future of our fishing industry. This motion is utter nonsense. I suggest a little more responsibility and serious concern is needed on the part of some hon. members opposite.
Mir. Woolliams: More reading.
Fisheries

The hon. member opposite seems to have had a bubbly dinner. In any event, it is a lovely spring day, and I am sure he enjoyed it. However, hon. members opposite seem to think they have a vested interest in destroying the effectiveness of the Canadian bargaining position. We are all Canadians, and the best bargaining position for Canada is something which cannot be played with and toyed with in the House.
Just as the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) proved himself to be a speculator's delight in his recent open-mouthed efforts to embarrass the government by single-handedly weakening the international credibility of the Canadian dollar, again we are faced with a position where some of our allegedly concerned individuals are in fact destructive tinkerers. Instead of attempting to single out the need for consultation as a government weakness, I suggest opposition parties should look carefully at their own performance in the House and try for the first time to fit into their personal vocabularies words like "co-operation" and "responsibility", and not criticize the full consultation which the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has initiated.

Mr. Speaker, in spite of what the minister has said, and in spite of what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) said earlier this afternoon, I have a group of clippings which indicate that there is no reasonable consultation, and if there is, it is after the fact rather than before.
An article in the Ottawa Citizen dated May 6, 1978 reads as follows:
Federal Fisheries Minister Romeo LeBlanc promised Friday to reconsider controversial regulations recently placed on Bay of Fundy scallop Fishermen.
Also his success is illustrated in the following headline, "Cdn. boats banned from U.S. West coast". Another headline reads, "Interim deal 'not binding' ". "Provinces still ask for power", "LeBlanc to review issue", and "Nfld. wants local fisheries control" are other headlines which I can use as examples.
I could go on, but I will not bore the House as time is of the essence at this particular moment. I suppose this evening's news gave the basic philosophical reason as to why this motion was brought forth. Although it does not particularly apply to the minister, it applies to the practices of the government in general. When Mrs. Ostry spoke tonight in order to receive her publicity, she stated that it was one thing to consult, it was one thing for people to make suggestions, but it did not necessarily mean the government had to take the suggestions. Perhaps a slight change in the phraseology of the motion is required. Perhaps hon. members opposite would care to amend it. But basically the consultative process has not functioned effectively or amicably between the Government of Canada and the various fishing ministries across the nation.
The predecessor to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has been criticized and blamed at various times in the House, but he initiated one program which was well worth while. It gave this House more information about the fishing

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
industry than it had gained in 25 years prior to the 1972-74 period. At that time, the minister of fisheries brought before the standing committee representatives of the seiners' associations, the weir fishermen's associations, the B.C. Fishing Association, the Newfoundland Fishing Association, the freshwater people from central Canada, and others. These people came before the committee and presented their briefs. We considered their problems. We were making an element of progress toward the solution of those problems.
This seemed to be embarrassing to the present minister. He does not want to see fishermen before the committee. He does not want the House of Commons to have the truth. He does not want the attitude of some members of the fishing industry toward his high-handed handling of this very important industry to be known. Since he has become minister, not a fisherman has had a voice before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry. We are kept with our blinders on.
