speechtext:
I may be in error only once since 1974. Perhaps they appeared once. It can be checked out and I stand to be corrected. I do not object to that. It was the general practice in 1972 to 1974. If fishermen have appeared before the committee to discuss their problems, it would be the exception since and not the rule as it was before. It was a good practice. It is the practice of virtually every other committee of the House. It is the practice of the Standing Committee on Agriculture to hear representations from the horticultural council and from the Federation of Agriculture. Why do we not hear from the fishermen in committee?
The minister has been aloof, inflexible and autocratic. He wants a maximum of organization and a minimum of constraint. The constraints appear in the fact that one cannot get a licence, and that people fish according to regulations which are very constrained. That does not work. The minister brought this motion on himself by creating inflexible situations, as well as by the unreasonable regulations which he has imposed at all levels of the fishing industry.
I should like to refer to a speech which the minister gave before the Fisheries Council of Canada. In part it reads as follows:
At a time of easy sales and of trade advantage for the dollar, I can understand those who feel that government has no business in the marketing plans of the nation. That is not my view. I have constantly insisted on the need for a strong Canadian presence in fish markets.
By that he meant a strong Canadian government presence. It continues:
We stand in the position of becoming the number one fish exporters in the world, or the owner of the world's largest fish warehouses.
We have had example after example of criticism by the Auditor General of the performance of Crown corporations in general. We have had particular criticism of two Crown corporations that are dealing specifically and solely with the

marketing of fish products from this nation. Both have been criticized and are under the scrutiny, to some degree, of the committee of the House of Commons. That committee chose in its wisdom to treat the matter firmly but briefly in the best interests of the fishing industry. I plead with the minister; let us take the proper position of government in respect of the marketing of this or any other commodity. Let us not get any further into Crown corporations marketing fish products. Do we want to have another AECL? Do we want another situation in which the fishermen do not know where their money has gone or why it has gone to international sales organizations in this world? That is a wrong position for governments to take.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
There are those who say this is the only way, but I find in the main that they have never sat behind a desk to conduct international trade in a multitude of countries. I have found that those who have sat in a managerial position and who understand the finesse that is needed to market products on an international basis are not those who say that the government should do the business. Again, I give to the fishermen the example of AECL. Just beware before you get involved in further Crown corporations.
The government should involve itself in the marketing process, but only to a degree. The government has at its disposal information which is not available to probably a single processor, and certainly not to a single fisherman or group of fishermen or fishermen's co-operatives. The government has that information which should be assimilated and put forward to all levels of the industry in an intelligent form which everybody can understand. The fishermen should know on a daily or weekly basis what the international markets of the world or the domestic markets of Canada or the United States will pay for a pound of fish. The fishermen should and must know this, and so should those who are marketing fish, whether they be brokers, processors or engaged in some other capacity in processing and marketing.
The Department of Agriculture does just this. It circulates market information so that at every level of the agricultural industry there is an understanding of what is the price today and the potential tomorrow. That is important and the government should co-operate with industry in this regard.
The government should activate the trade commissions of this country in the one hundred or more countries in which they are located. Those trade commissioners should be told that, as fish is one of our major potential exports, as the minister has said, and I agree, they should get up out of their plush-lined chairs and get out and sell agriculture products, fish products and manufactured products. They should be told that is their job, that they should find out what is the potential in their markets, what is the price there, and send that information back home to advise our people what is available in those areas. That is what the government should do to help everybody.
May 11, 1978

1 do not think one needs to expand on that. The government in virtually every aspect of Canadian business has been negligent as it has tried to expand the markets for Canadian goods and services world wide, and it has been particularly negligent in promoting the sale of agricultural and fish products.
The statistics which come to hand would indicate we have a declining catch of quite a number of species important to the Canadian fishing industry. The fisherman is asking why we have this declining catch and does not have the answer. The research scientist does not seem to have the answer. When you go to the research stations around this nation the scientists cannot give you the exact answer. The fishermen are asking questions which I think should be answered. Is the answer that the stocks are declining? If a stock is declining, is that because there are too many Canadian licences or are we granting too many foreign licences? Is the Canadian fisherman getting enough licences for the stocks that exist or could there be more of them so we can increase the catch in that way? Could we cut back some-not cut out but cut back-on quantities which are extended within our 200-mile limit to other nations? Is there too little surveillance? Perhaps there are not too many licences issued to foreign fishermen, but is there enough surveillance? Do we know now any better than before what the foreign fleet is catching?
Is there too much incidental catch? We do know that for some reason or other in an area where salmon fishing is not legal you can get Atlantic salmon in any restaurant between Montreal and Sydney. You cannot legally fish salmon for sale, but you can sell incidental catch. The people who are interested in the salmon industry want to know how come there is such a major supply of incidentally caught salmon which you can eat in the restaurants of this nation. The Government of Canada is still paying the commercial salmon fishermen not to fish, yet there is still salmon for sale. Is it correct, as rumour would suggest, that we do have an organized salmon sales organization? Is it correct that if you catch thirty salmon incidentally in a net today there is no problem selling them beneficially before nightfall? That is more than a rumour and it requires investigation by the minister and his staff.
What we do know is that while the minister is continuing to pay millions of dollars so that commercial salmon fishermen do not fish there is no surveillance along the rivers and streams which effectively prevents commercial poaching structures that exist in the fresh water system of Atlantic Canada and eastern Quebec. Is there a comparable poaching problem in the salt water nearby the shores of eastern Canada? It would seem that there may well be.
Why are there declining stocks and declining catches? The fishermen's income is not that bad. As a matter of fact, in most instances the income is very good. However, I do think Canada should be concerned about the decline in the pounds of fish caught, and the minister should be doing his best within market capabilities to see that we recover the poundage of catch we had so we can get back into fishing those people who have left in the last ten years.
Fisheries
The minister suggested how great the industry is. He mentioned the wrong era. In the era he mentioned of the 1950s and the 1960s a man could get assistance from the Government of Canada in the form of a subsidy to buy a boat. He could get a licence, and in spite of the fact that prices were lower the fishermen often paid for a $300,000, $400,000 or $500,000 seiner in three, four or five years with special concessions from the income tax branch, also granted by the government.
Today you could not afford to build a boat if you wanted to, because you could not get a subsidy. If you did build a boat, you could not get a licence as you could in former days, and it is highly improbable that you could get a special permit from the department of internal revenue in order to pay off the cost of that boat in a short period of time. The circumstances which made that an expansion era in the fishing industry in the Bay of Fundy have now ended. You cannot get a licence and you cannot buy a boat. The fishermen are getting more money but their seines cost three times as much, their nets for weirs cost three times as much and fuel costs more than three times as much. The number of subsidies is down and the amount of income tax is up. It is just about time the Government of Canada took a long, hard look at the real income of some of these fishermen. We have to get back into the fishing industry and we have to issue more licences.
We have got to allow people to improve their boats, restore a reasonable level of subsidy from the Government of Canada, and become more aware of the consultative processes that are necessary so that the federal and provincial governments can co-operate in the planning of a resource which in Atlantic Canada's mind is as much theirs as is the oil of Alberta. The one belongs to the one as much as the one belongs to the other. You cannot regulate the oil of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or British Columbia. You can tax it to death, and the government just about has, but still maintains control. The Minister of Fisheries is determined that he will maintain absolute control of the water resources of fish, minerals and whatever else may be under the surface. To a degree that is inexcusable and unacceptable. As long as he wishes to use that high-handed authority of his, there will not be contentment on the subject anywhere in Atlantic Canada.

sails clear across the Pacific Ocean and either around the tip of South America or through the Panama Canal and up the Atlantic seaboard of North America, and it fishes those fish which would not be profitable for Canada. Having travelled that far it is still profitable. I want an explanation, and a detailed explanation, as to why that boat would not be used profitably if it was Canadian owned. It is a very fragile story that the minister told us this afternoon in respect to that facet of the fishing structure.
In view of the number of people who would like to express their views in this debate, I am not going to go any further tonight. As the member from Newfoundland stated, if you had until midnight tonight you would not have said it all, and you could not have said it all. I have said enough to prove that the consultative process is necessary, that a comprehension of the industry in the ministry is necessary, that both are lacking and that the consultation is after the fact and conducted in bad feeling, as it was in Nova Scotia, as it is in Newfoundland and as it has been in eastern Canada, central Canada and western Canada. The fishing industry in Canada cannot reach the peak it should as long as a process of autocratic confrontation or consultation after the fact exists. The irritation remains. If that policy does not come to an end, the Canadian fishing industry cannot achieve the level of success which it deserves and which the fishermen in particular deserve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate. First of all, I want to correct the record on at least one thing that the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said. He said there were no more subsidies on fishing vessels. That, at least in my province, is not true. The subsidies still exist. There is a 35 per cent subsidy still in effect on boats between 30 feet and 45 feet and boats between 60 feet and 65 feet. As a matter of fact, an additional amount of $250,000 was put into Newfoundland from Canada Works funds this past winter for job creation purposes. The subsidy still exists on vessels and longliners, plus there is still a subsidy from industry, trade and commerce on vessels over 75 feet.
This motion seems to have more to do with personalities than with the substance of policy. I do not know if that is because the opposition feels that the policy is good as it stands-I certainly do-but I feel the emphasis is on personality and the failure to consult. But even there I find an ambivalence, because the hon. member for St. John's West began and ended by saying that this was the greatest Minister of Fisheries since 1949, excluding Tory ministers of which there have not been very many since 1949. However, in the middle of his speech he said everything that this minister has done was wrong. He has not done anything right. I cannot see how that is a consistent argument.
One of the arguments the opposition is making is that the minister is failing to consult with the provinces. I heard the phrase this evening, "We are not going to be dictated to by the Ottawa bureaucracy". If you look at the bureaucracy within the fisheries service in Ottawa, you will find that a great many of them are in fact Newfoundlanders, people who lived by the

sea, grew up by the sea and made themselves expert in fishing. Some of our top negotiators and policy makers within the fisheries department are from Newfoundland.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: Name some.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
I can name them but it is not the practice to name such people in the House. I will be glad, however, to send the hon. member a list of these people within the fishery service who I am talking about. In fact, somebody last week from Atlantic Canada said, "We are no longer going to be dictated to by the Newfoundland mafia in Ottawa." Check your papers and you will find the quote, "Newfoundland mafia". Hon. members cannot have it both ways. You cannot say on the one hand that you are being dictated to by a foreign bureaucracy in Ottawa when in fact there is adequate evidence that fisheries policy, apart form the political level, is being constructed by Newfoundlanders, born and bred and well educated.
The opposition is talking about consultation and the minister's failure to consult. My friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) put on the record reams and reams-and I have them in front of me now-of consultations that the ministry of fisheries held. I do not hear the president of the fishermen's union in Newfoundland saying that he has not been consulted, although I do hear the minister of fisheries from Newfoundland saying that he has not been consulted.
I am also told that this subject is not political and has nothing to do with politics. We have a minister from Nova Scotia of one political stripe and a minister from Newfoundland of another political stripe. Obviously, these people are Simon pure and are the Robin Hoods of eastern Canada, and they are not doing this for political purposes. Well, if there is no politics involved why is it I have not got on my desk this great $900 million plan? Nor do the hon. member for Bonavis-ta-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Rooney), the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) or the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) have it on their desks. If there is no politics, why have we not been consulted?
I am a Newfoundlander and I have some rights. I may not have the total say in shaping the policy, but I have some say. If there is this lack of consultation on the part of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc), why is it that the minister of fisheries from Newfoundland has not seen fit to consult any Newfoundlanders in Ottawa? He cannot have it both ways. He cannot say on the one hand that we are not consulting with him if, on the other hand, he is not consulting with us. And he is not. I challenge him to show me a letter, any speech that he has given or any document from him that is in my possession. If somebody can find that I would be pleased to see it. We have not been consulted.
The fact is the only people who saw that document were the press. It was a political episode, and I think that it should be viewed in that light. The provincial ministers were playing politics with the issue. They saw that things were good and they wanted to get on the bandwagon; therefore they took this tack. I do not think it was a very positive or creative tack, but


May 11, 1978

if they want to play games that way then that is their prerogative. The plain and simple fact is that that episode of the plan of the Atlantic provinces, which was not paid attention to in Ottawa, was in my opinion a political episode.
In the long run one may be able to fool members of parliament, the cabinet, bureaucrats and even the press. No, I would not go so far as to say you can fool the press. But there is one other group that you cannot fool, and that is the fishermen. The fishermen realize that this Minister of Fisheries, if he is anything, is not a minister of fisheries but of fishermen. There is adequate proof of that.
As well as saying that they are not being consulted, the provinces are saying that they want more control. I think we have to be very, very careful about that and continue to see that resource as a Canadian resource. I do not think we can consider the resource as being Newfoundland fish, Nova Scotia fish or British Columbia fish; where would we stop? If that concept were taken a little farther the stocks would have to be split up and somehow divided.
The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) read some press clippings during this debate which said that the provinces want control and authority over the fishery. But if they were to get that authority would they, in turn, appoint an authority over each bay? In Newfoundland, for example, if the minister of fisheries there were to get authority over the province, would be then turn authority over the stocks in Labrador to the people of Labrador?
The hon. member for St. John's West said that Newfoundland now has a great fisheries department and that he built it up. I give him credit for that-credit where credit is due. He did. At the present time, however, they do not have one single provincial fisheries officer in Labrador. If anybody can find one and identify him for me, I would be glad to see him, but as far as I know, there is not one. If they have such a great department and are going to exercise authority, when are they going to appoint some officials?
I do not think you can take that argument to its ultimate conclusion because it means a balkanization, splitting up rather than working together. I believe we should see this as a Canadian resource. I also feel that the people who are contiguous to the resource should have the primary chance to harvest the stock. I think that is also the minister's view. It seems to me that to balkanize the fishery would lead us into very deep water indeed. This is a time when we should act together as Canadians and not balkanize.
The minister has not only been accused of not consulting but also of not initiating a policy for the protection and development of the Canadian fishing industry. I said that this was a minister of fishermen. This is the government and this is the minister that brought in the 200-mile limit. I also said that you could not fool the fishermen. Do not try to tell fishermen along the northeast coast of Newfoundland that the fishery has been mismanaged, and in particular do not tell them that when fish
Fisheries
landings have gone up by 30 to 40 per cent. They will find it difficult to believe that the fishery has been mismanaged.
This is the minister who a couple of years ago, when the fishing industry in this country was in trouble because Korea had hit the United States market with some cheaper fish and outbid us in that market upon which we are so dependent, obtained almost $200 million from the government to shore up the Atlantic fishing industry until he could develop an effective policy.
This is the minister who for the first time put subsidies in the pockets of fishermen. Until a couple of years ago it was the fish companies-the merchant princes of Water Street-who received the subsidies in the province of Newfoundland. Two years ago, two cents per pound on top quality groundfish went to the fishermen for the first time. This is not the Minister of Fisheries, this is the minister of fishermen. This is the minister who has put subsidies on new vessels, who has continued to build marine facilities all around the coast of Atlantic and Pacific Canada. This is the minister who has stressed the inshore fishery as opposed to the offshore.
The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte spoke of the advent of more freezer trawlers. He should recognize, when that sort of thing happens, that if you increase the offshore fleet you simply replace the foreign fishing effort with a Canadian effort that will be in direct competition with Canadian inshore fishermen. It has been the policy of this government to stress the importance of the inshore fishery-as a matter of fact, to take off the top of the groundfish quota every year, a percentage for the inshore fishery. I think the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte should remember the competition that more freezer trawlers for the offshore fleet would provide for the inshore fishery.
The latest policy for the improvement of facilities is a four-year $13 million program to equip about 200 ports with such things as net-bags, hoists and freezer containers to ensure top quality inshore fisheries.
This is the minister, Mr. Speaker, who very dramatically in the past couple of years stood up to world opinion on the matter of the seal hunt. I did not hear anyone on the other side of the House mention that today, although for the last three years the government and opposition have been battling jointly to get the law changed. In all fairness I think that should have been mentioned today and some credit given where it was due.
This is the minister who did not cave in, who did not get weak knees at the expression of adverse public opinion across the world and who changed the law to give greater protection to sealers who depend on that resource for part of their livelihood.
This is the minister who was building new research vessels and who has encouraged research in stocks off our shores. The shrimp, for example, has been described by some people as a virtual gold mine, and it is hoped that in the next couple of years we will begin harvesting shrimp and scallop and other species that we have not harvested up to now. I hope the

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
minister will be making a statement on that in the next few days.
Then there is the matter of ownership of the fleet. The minister has said that his policy leads to ownership by fishermen of a greater part of the fishing fleet. The result is that, where appropriate, ownership of some part of the fleet by processing companies may decrease. This policy is intended to establish all fishing vessels as profit centres which would lead to the development of a better port market-pricing system for landings of fish.
Along with the independent ownership of vessels by fishermen, the minister has proposed credit requirements. In recognition of the fact that the resource availability will continue to improve and that the industry is on the road to development, the minister is saying that a requirement for credit financing could be expected for new and replacement facilities, including vessels. It is his intention to promote the development of a credit institution which will satisfy this requirement. It is intended that the credit institution will play an important role in implementing the policy to encourage independent fishermen to own vessels. This is important to fishermen. They do not have it now; it is something they should have and something the minister is working toward.
The next concern is increasing the Canadian share of the catch. We have heard tonight that foreigners are continually fishing off our shores, but that is a bit of a myth, Mr. Speaker. Primarily the fish they catch is fish that we as Canadians are not able to catch anyway. What have we done about the Canadian share of the catch since the 200-mile limit was imposed? The Canadian government has set quotas for 1978 that will keep foreigners almost completely out of our traditional fisheries such as cod, herring, haddock and redfish. In the cod fishery of southern Labrador and eastern Newfoundland where a few years ago foreigners took over 650,000 metric tonnes, they will now have a quota of 35,000 metric tonnes for 1978 whereas Canadians will harvest 100,000 metric tonnes. The remaining foreign quotas will be almost all in species that Canada does not fish in any great amount- silver hake, capelin, argentine and so on.
The minister has also instituted other programs for the supply of ice which again helps to produce quality fish. I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. There is the matter of additional quotas for inshore fishermen and policies to protect them. There are other policies which are coming into being and which we on this side of the House will help establish.
I think it is unfortunate that this particular motion deals with personalities rather than the substance of policy. The evidence is there with regard to the policy; the evidence is there with regard to the performance of this government and this minister particularly. He is seen by the fishermen to be their minister. That is not only evidenced in his policy but in the way he conducts himself. While it may be possible to fool some of the people some of the time, it is not possible to fool the fishermen in this instance. It must be abundantly clear by now that if there were a vote tonight, I would vote against this motion.
Mir. Stan Darling (Parry Sound-Muskoka): Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a brief contribution to this very timely motion introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). The concern expressed in the motion is very genuine and has been very eloquently endorsed by a number of my colleagues.
The two areas of deep concern outlined in this motion affect all Canadians, whether they live on the east coast, the west coast or in central Canada. The total lack of a consultative process between the federal Department of Fisheries and its provincial counterparts and the failure to develop a positive policy for the protection and development of the Canadian fishing industry is disturbing, to say the least.
I would also like to debunk the myth that the fishing industry is somehow the domain of our two coastal communities. We in central Canada, and in Ontario in particular, do indulge in fishing in pursuit of leisure. On the other hand, the commercial fishing industry offers employment to about 4,000 to 5,000 people and the catch is close to 40 million pounds a year. Currently the cash flow from this very important and growing industry is in the vicinity of $20 million for landed catch. This could be doubled to $40 million in retail sales.
These statistics, in a very small way, underscore my earlier remark about the importance of commercial fishing in the province of Ontario. We on this side of the House make an urgent plea to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) to embark on some long-range and constructive policies in collaboration with his provincial counterparts in order to inject some life into an industry which is currently on weak economic ground. There need to be some constructive policies adopted in the area of fisheries resource management.
We in central Canada must join our coastal colleagues in this House who represent some thriving fishing communities on both coasts to express our concern about the violation of our 200-mile territorial limit. We have been very fortunate to enjoy an extremely amiable relationship with our southern neighbour. It will be a tragedy if we succumb to petty territorial rivalries with our neighbours and friends over commercial interests in fishing. It behooves the government, Mr. Speaker, to take urgent and positve action in engaging in serious and genuine consultations with our southern neighbour. The urgency and seriousness of the matter has been profoundly underscored in the past few days by my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro).
My apprehension stems from the fact that this government may oversee the demise of our illustrious fishing industry in precisely the same manner in which it ruined our shipbuilding industry. The government's policy in the area of fisheries is shortsighted and erratic, similar to the deficient and bankrupt policies being implemented by the government to deal with our economic woes.
We are not asking the government to perform miracles. The fishing industry needs and certainly deserves a long-range plan of action which will introduce some form of stability, in

May 11, 1978

contrast to the patchwork policies being pursued by the Department of Fisheries.
This morning I had the privilege of sitting as a member of the external affairs committee when the estimates of CIDA were being debated and questioned. The witness before the committee was Mr. Dupuy, the president of CIDA. It is interesting to note that that branch of external affairs has a budget of $1.2 billion, which was dealt with in less that two hours because of the present committee set-up. I am sure the president will not be back before the committee and the estimates will be deemed to be passed as of the end of this month.
I bring this to the attention of the House because in that over $1 billion of estimates there was one small item of $32 million which was earmarked for ten fishing projects. I certainly find no fault with CIDA projects to help countries in the third world. Part of that amount will be used for agricultural development, food. Part will be used to improve the fishery, part to provide boats, small boats, I believe, rather than the very expensive boats which CIDA provided in past years. Another part of the money will be used for fishing schools and training and also for outboard motors.
These projects worth $32 million are earmarked for this year, provided the third world countries and Canada work out suitable arrangements, which I certainly expect they will. There are also projects in the amount of $26 million on the board for the future.
The province I represent, Ontario, receives only $4 million of the entire budget of the Department of Fisheries, less than 9 per cent. One little department of CIDA will receive three and a half times that amount. The combined revenues of the commercial fishery and sports fishery of Ontario equals the amount of revenue generated by either of the coasts. Members on either side of the House may look at this askance, but that is correct. The province of Ontario is probably not assumed to be a commercial fishing province. I wanted that mentioned specifically.
Ontario has 25 per cent of the fresh water in Canada, several thousand miles of shoreline and approximately 53 per cent of all the small craft in Canada. There are 455 harbours. Granted, a good many are recreational harbours, but a good number are dual harbours.
Ontario is getting short-changed with regard to the amount of money allocated, considering that Ontario has more shoreline than the province of Quebec. However, the Quebec allotment is greater than Ontario. That does not even include the allocated amount for the Montreal harbour. I was under the impression that was around $26 million, but someone mentioned it is closer to $40 million. In addition, a tremendous amount is earmarked for Quebec City.
The province of Ontario contributes a considerable amount to the national coffers, but gets the short end of the stick when the Department of Fisheries and the Environment is handing out money. It is very important that Ontario at least get its
Fisheries
share. As I mentioned before, it should at least get half its share.
We are talking about commercial fishing, but sport fishing is also important. It generates amounts in the millions of dollars. It is estimated that Ontario has 53 per cent of all pleasure boats in Canada. Our dual harbours are used for both commercial fishing and tourism. It is therefore important that the provinces should have additional moneys available with which to improve facilities. I have received letters from municipalities requesting improvements to docks. The regional manager of Environment Canada in charge of small harbours informs me that he appreciates the situation but that the available budget is cut to the bone and no additional funds are available. A few days ago I contacted the department because one of the municipalities had requested improvements to the docks. The regional manager said that nothing could be done before 1979-80.
So here again we find the little province of Ontario, which is contributing greatly to federal revenues, in a less than favourable position. I see hon. members smiling. I say it is just as well to have it on record. Everybody seems to think Ontario is the most favoured province, but a good many other provinces are fortunate that Ontario is able to contribute such large amounts of money in so many directions.
Tourism is another important means of generating money. I draw attention to the fact that there are 110 million Americans living within one day's drive of Ontario. And don't think they are not coming over here in droves. Naturally, we would like to see them coming in even greater numbers to help make Ontario and Canada green, but to encourage this movement it is important that we have the facilities they need, including upgraded harbours.
I will close, now, Mr. Speaker, realizing that there are others who wish to contribute to the debate this evening.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in the debate this evening, consideration of a motion which condemns the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc), allegedly because there has been a lack of consultation. I do not want to spend much time on that part of the motion because the minister himself and his parliamentary secretary have dealt with it adequately. The minister tabled this afternoon a list of the meetings and consultations in which he has taken part, together with provincial representatives, fishermen's groups and other organizations. It is a record unmatched by any other minister.
Not only has the present minister been the best Minister of Fisheries, as the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) admitted this evening, but he has consulted more widely with provincial governments and others before reaching decisions. As I say, I do not want to spend too much time on the consultation aspect because it seems to me the opposition speakers were not particularly interested in it; they were more interested in finding other grounds for criticizing the minister.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: All those governments aren't Liberal. You are judging them all by yourself.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
All those governments are not Liberal, but the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and all their inshore fishermen would become bankrupt if we were to accept the plan put forward by the province of Newfoundland, with the support of the province of Nova Scotia, because they do not want to rebuild the stocks. They are not concerned about proper management or rational development. I have a copy of their plan here. They want to build fishing capacity beyond what it was before the 200-mile limit was set. They want to build it beyond what it was when foreigners were fishing there. They are not talking about rebuilding stocks either in the 200-mile limit or in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. What they want to do is rape the resource and get short-term profits for themselves.
I think that point of view should be put to the people of this country and to the people of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. I would be very happy for them if they could get something good, but there is a problem. The question is not one of who should own the resource but of who can manage it properly. I am from the Atlantic provinces, but we must criticize ourselves because, while we might agree in criticizing Ottawa or the rest of the country, the four Atlantic provinces cannot agree on the time of day. The maritime provinces have been trying for the last few years to agree on something. Why all these inter-governmental meetings between provinces when really one constitutional authority can listen to the four Atlantic provinces?
The federal authority has to account to this House and to hon. members opposite, who do not consider themselves the protectors of the interests of their constituents. They do not consider themselves the protectors of the interests of the people
May 11, 1978

of Newfoundland or Nova Scotia. I do, and I am also ready to defend the interests of my constituents at any time in this House. Is it not really more efficient and does it not make more sense to have one constitutional authority? In the Gulf of St. Lawrence or even outside the gulf we really cannot define the line between the provinces of New Brunswick, Quebec, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. And what do we do about P.E.I.? How are we going to agree on the line?
The position put forward by the province of Newfoundland is unfair in terms of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The people of New Brunswick depend on the rebuilding of stocks and on a rational and cautious development of that fishery in the future. However, the position accepted by the Conservative opposition is really unworkable, and to suggest that we could bring together the four Atlantic provinces and the province of Quebec even to agree on where to hold a meeting to discuss these things is absurd. Nobody would agree on anything. As I said before, they could not even agree on the time of day. The result would be that a few companies based in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland would rape the resource.
We all know the concentration of power presently in the fishing industry. We all know about the transfer of shares which took place on the stock market in 1977. We all know how strong fishing companies are becoming. We all know that while provincial politicians were arguing amongst themselves, five or six big companies would rape the resource, and the result would be that all of us would pay very dearly.
I just hope that the Conservative party comes before the people in the Atlantic provinces with that kind of position, because I feel that the people of Canada everywhere do want a stronger central government; and if there is one area where the fishermen and the people generally want the federal government to maintain its authority, it is the area of resource management for the fishery. Anything else would be total chaos.
The basis of the policy of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment in the last few years has been to have a fair allocation of quotas. For the first time in the last two years we have an allocation of quotas. If there is going to be a scarcity of fish, we say that different areas will have a fair allocation of quota. They can extract that fish from the sea. However, we also say that inshore fishermen will have their share. How will they have their share if more than one authority decides how much fish is to be taken? If we do not protect fish coming into the Gulf of St. Lawrence by having a sound, rational and cautious development policy within the 200-mile limit, it just will not get there. If it does not get there, that will mean bankruptcy for the fishing industry. The basis of the policy of cautious development is that the inshore fishermen should have a share and an opportunity to enjoy the prosperity it had, in relative terms, 20 years ago.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: I agree with that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte now says he agrees. It is difficult to understand the policy of the Conservative party. One wonders if it is the result of conviction
Fisheries
or confusion. Just about 20 minutes ago the hon. member was criticizing the minister for saying exactly what I am saying. I am saying that we should resist the policy of the Newfoundland government. Just because it is a Tory government, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte should not think it has the divine answer to everything. I am here defending the minister and explaining why, and the hon. member interjects and says he agrees. The hon. member should make up his mind.
I should remind the hon. member about what has been happening to the herring fishery in his own constituency in the last few years. The purse-seine landings tripled in value in 1977 over 1975, from $2.8 million to about $7 million, yet he has the gall to criticize the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. The minister saved the herring fishery in the Bay of Fundy with his policy. Federal government measures have tripled the value of the herring purse-seine fishery in the Bay of Fundy. Federal fisheries authorities backed the seiners to form a marketing co-operative and helped them work out individual boat quotas which enabled them to slow down their rate of fishing and to sell herring for processing into food rather than racing to catch all the quota in a short time to sell for reduction to fishmeal. That is what was happening before the minister came in with his policy.
The hon. member suggests that the federal government is unfair by insisting that it should have the authority to regulate the fishery. He should have been in his constituency over the last two months asking herring fishermen what they think about that. If the herring fishermen of the hon. member's constituency were to read his speech of this evening, I would have to go there to help him in the next election because he would be in difficulty.
I mentioned a while ago that in 1978 Canada will get 69 per cent of the traditional groundfish catch. In 1974 it got only 33 per cent. That is not the only difference we must look at. In terms of inshore fisheries, again for the first time the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment introduced the concept of allocation on a regional basis. For example, there will be a cod quota in 1978 for the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Not only will there be a cod quota generally for the Atlantic provinces but also for the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Also there is a cod quota for inshore fishermen. As a result of that, the inshore fisheries now have an opportunity to prosper.
For hon. members opposite, under the guise of a motion, to attempt to condemn the minister for lack of consultation is unreasonable. They come here and present various arguments. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) complained this afternoon about 500 licences being given to foreign fishing vessels within the 200-mile limit. Is that a big scandal? In the groundfish industry, we will be fishing 69 per cent in 1978, whereas in 1974 we were fishing only 32 per cent of the total allowable catch. The foreigners are receiving species which Canada is not equipped to process. Canada is not used to

May 11, 1978
Fisheries
fishing those species traditionally, and we do not have a market for them. Why not let the foreigners take them?
I support the position of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. I support his contention that fisheries management must remain a federal authority.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext: At this time in our history, there is no way that I would want to see the central government weakened in any way, particularly not in the area of the fisheries. That would mean chaos. There is no way the four Atlantic provinces would agree on anything. The result would be that four or five big companies would control the fisheries. For an hon. member from New Brunswick to suggest that the power over fisheries should be given to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia is not feasible. The result would be that the inshore fisheries of New Brunswick would be totally bankrupt. I could not stand for that. I support the posture the minister has taken, as well as the policy which he introduced respecting a cautious development of the fisheries. If there is a need for more fishing capacity, better boats and bigger boats, later on we can acquire these boats when necessary and when there are fish to fish in the sea.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NECESSITY FOR CONSULTATION ON FISHERY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the very few minutes remaining in our allotted day, I should like to speak about the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. It was established in 1969 specifically to market fish, fish products and by-products in the Northwest Territories, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and a portion of Ontario. As is clearly stated in its 1976-1977 annual report, the objective of the corporation was to market fish in an orderly manner and to increase interprovincial and export trade.
One could probably write a book on the allegations which have been brought to our attention concerning this corporation over the past eight months. One such allegation is that 14 million to 15 million pounds of fish purchased by the corporation through its Transcona plant were in storage at a cost of $5,000 a day to the fishermen. Some of it has been kept in storage for as long as nine months. Another allegation was that many pounds of fillets had to be thrown away because of freezer burn. A further allegation concerned the deliberate changing of packaging dates on fish already in storage so that it would appear to be fresh fish. Apparently expensive fishing and processing equipment was sitting unused adjacent to the Transcona plant. I could refer to many such allegations.
Prior to the estalishment of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, fishermen sold their produce through various private companies in the north. At that time all the fish was being sold. It did not have to be put into storage, and the fishermen were not assessed some nine cents a pound per annum to keep fish in storage. Today the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation does not seem able to sell half the amount of fish being produced. From 1963 to 1969 the average production in northern Manitoba was nine million pounds per annum. That fish was all marketed. It did not have to be

stored, and fishermen were not assessed one cent per pound per month. Now that the corporation is in place, the average annual market volume is 5.5 million pounds. We have taken a step backward.
The corporation will indicate that fishermen are receiving a better price for their catch, but when fishermen are required to pay in order to keep fish in storage for a period up to nine months, that theory does not make sense. Instead of putting this fish in storage, we should use mother nature's deep freeze. The lakes in northern Manitoba are ideal. In the wintertime they could be used to replace deep freezer storage until production is sold to a buyer in the United States, our major customer. The fish could be taken out of the lakes and shipped directly to the market. Then fishermen would receive a better price for their fish, at least ten cents a pound bonus for fishing in the wintertime. Also we would get away from these high storage costs.
If the Canadian inland fishery is to survive, we will have to take a look at the lakeside results which fishermen receive in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, the Northwest Territories and so on. A portion of Ontario has opted out of the program. The fishermen of that province are now receiving $1.16 to $1.20 per pound for pickerel, whereas fishermen under the corporation receive only 50 cents to 69 cents per pound.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, on May 3 I directed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). I asked her whether representations had been made by medical researchers to the effect that the small increase in funds allocated for medical research this year would have very serious effects on the entire program of medical research, and on the ability of this country to keep medical research in Canada. The minister replied by pointing out that there had been an increase of 5.6 per cent, which amounted to approximately $60 million. Also in view of the freeze under the restraint program, she felt that medical researchers had not been badly dealt with.
May 11, 1978

The increase is far short of what is required. Medical education in Canada to a large extent has been based on teachers in our medical colleges who are vitally interested and tremendously involved in research in the various specialties for which they have been trained and are deeply involved. They are experts in their fields. They want to continue their work. If they are not permitted to continue their work because funds are not made available, they will move to the United States. The United States is not just a country close to Canada, not just a country to which it is easy to move, and not just a country in which the people speak the same language; it is a country which spends at least ten times as much per capita on medical research as we in Canada spend.
This results in a constant pull from Canada of Canadian medical researchers to the United States. Just a week or so ago one of the best known and most competent of the researchers at the medical college at the University of Manitoba, Dr. Ruben Cherniack, announced he would be moving to one of the mid-western states. He is moving because he does not have to worry in that state about the funding necessary to carry on the research in which he is interested. The money is made available there freely and willingly.
Too little money for medical research has been the story for many years in Canada. What have aggravated the situation are the stop and go programs in Canada. Some two years ago when medical researchers successfully mounted a protest against that year's cut-backs, the then minister of national health and welfare, speaking at a meeting of the Standing Committee of Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, said in part:
You cannot just turn it on and off as if it were a water tap. What we are trying to develop is a kind of formula or criterion, by which research... particularly medical research ... will be able to count on some reasonably steady rate of growth in its expenditures.
Those were brave and sensible words. The medical research community hoped the government had changed its thinking and that there was a new understanding regarding the importance of medical reasearch. They thought the government had accepted the principles enunciated in those words I have just quoted from the former minister. After two relatively good years, researchers find this year they are right back in the mess they were in two years ago. The $60 million allocated is just not good enough. This is an increase and we can argue how much. The minister said it was an increase of 5.6 per cent. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in a letter said it was an increase of 7.8 per cent, and medical researchers say it is an increase of three decimal something per cent. The fact is that the cost of medical research has gone up between 15 per cent and 20 per cent annually.
What this small increase this year means is that the National Research Council had to turn down about 167 grants for highly qualified applicants, as well as the applications of 32 excellent investigators who wanted to continue the work which has been funded by the National Research Council so far. They have been told they would have to conclude their research in the next few months. It has been estimated that
Adjournment Debate
they need about another $6 million to cover the cost of staffing their research programs, as well as for equipment and for the development grants program which has gone a long way to providing the salary support needed to recruit new faculty members in the newer medical colleges. This development grants program was cut to the bone. It is short by at least $500,000.
What we have according to medical researchers is another crisis which will have a profound effect not just on the researchers but on the whole program of medical education. What we are talking about is some $6 million, and I do not believe that a country like Canada which has programs in every field which total in the tens of billions of dollars cannot find $6 million. I would urge the minister to reconsider the decision.
The Acting Speaking (Mr. Ethier): Order, please.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) for bringing up at this time a topic which is not only of concern to him but to many other members of parliament, and certainly to the Minister of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I would like to point out to him that the minister did reply to him in her response of May 3, 1978, but I wish to amplify that to some extent. Before doing so, however, although he has mentioned that many doctors are moving to the United States, I would like to inform him that it is not all milk and honey and sweetness and light in the United States and many doctors are returning.
The hon. member also indicated that the per capita research in the United States is ten times that of Canada. If he checks his figures he will find it is not ten times the per capita amount but rather $10 per capita in the United States as compared to one-third of that in Canada, if my figures are correct. It is true there is a difference, but ten times as against three times is quite a significant difference.
I disagree with the hon. member when he says there is a crisis as far as this is concerned, because many of the most important projects are in fact being funded at the present time. I believe that many hon. members will have received representations from their constituencies about the government's funding of medical research in 1978-79. I appreciate and share that concern.
I would like to take this opportunity, however, to correct a number of inaccuracies that have crept into reports and statements in the media. It has been stated that 20 per cent of ongoing Canadian projects in the medical sector have just been terminated by the Medical Research Council. This is significant exaggeration which should be corrected. In Canada in the fiscal year just ended, a total of 2,725 research projects in medical fields were under way with support from one of the major granting agencies-federal, provincial or voluntary.

May 11, 1978
Adjournment Debate
This figure included 1,302 supported by the federal Medical Research Council, of which 545 were assured of funding for the coming year without further review.
In November, 1977, and March, 1978, the Medical Research Council had for consideration applications for the renewal of 575 projects. Approval was given to continued support of 475 of those projects for further periods of one to three years. In the remaining 100 cases, support was provided only for periods of three to eight months, to enable the investigators to bring the projects to an orderly conclusion or to revise the protocol for future work so that it would be more favourably viewed by the applicant's scientific peers and thus receive further funding in the next competition. This unconditional award rate of 82 per cent of the requests under review is not at all unusual in the experience of the Medical Research Council.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-CONSTRUCTION OF FACILITIES AT CHARLOTTETOWN-ALLEGED DELAY FOR ECONOMIC REASONS
AIRPORTS-CONSTRUCTION OF FACILITIES AT CHARLOTTETOWN-ALLEGED DELAY FOR ECONOMIC REASONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may make a minor transgression from procedure, I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary to convey to his minister my opinion that she is a lady of great compassion, and I support her in all the endeavours that she has put forward for the deserving people of this country.
Once again I address the House on a problem both important and pressing, the construction of adequate airport facilities for the city of Charlottetown and the province of Prince Edward Island. This is not the first time I have presented my concerns, Mr. Speaker. I brought up the subject most recently on November 7, 1977, and on May 24 and January 31 of the same year. I had hoped that an announcement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on November 8, 1977 concerning funding for the new terminus would have ended my anxiety. However, I fear that my worries are far from alleviated. Delay and uncertainty seem to remain the order of the day.
The problems we are facing become increasingly serious as we approach the summer months. Tourists will soon be heading to our beautiful villages and sunny beaches. Once again the summer visitor arriving by air will be greeted with uncomfortable and inadequate convenience-an unnecessary and unwelcome set of circumstances far from becoming the capital city of the province where confederation began.
9 (2212)
Being a believer in representative democracy, I consider it a grave situation that the worries of the people of the village of East Royalty have not been eased. For months they have had to contend with uncertainty concerning their position in respect to their property. Certainly, land acquisition is a necessary effect of expanding the Charlottetown airport. It has been estimated that approximately 28 property owners will be affected by the project, 28 individuals and families who at the

present time have not been given any reasonable assurance from the federal government as to their circumstances or their future. They had been promised ample opportunity through public meetings to voice their position and to receive information from the responsible officials. The last such public session was held in December of last year, with no indication of another forthcoming. The people of East Royalty are deserving of better treatment and I request of the minister that the village be given immediate recognition and full information so that this problem affecting the airport's expansion be resolved.
Not all Islanders are enthusiastic about the Charlottetown airport plan. On a "hot line" radio program in Charlottetown, some citizens have suggested that $21 million is too much to spend. I know this problem and I am convinced of the importance of new air terminal facilities to the economy of the province and the well-being of its citizens. The sum of $21 million is not too much; in fact, I wonder if it is too little. We of the Island have been too long neglected. I urge the minister not to consider a reduction of this figure. PEI deserves a first class airport and I make no apology for advocating such an installation. Why should we settle for second best? I think we should not.
Four weeks ago we all thought that the days of this parliament were numbered. After today's words from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) it seems that we are to stay for yet another few months. I urge the minister to devote some of this freshly acquired time to the exigencies of the construction of this much needed facility and to go "full steam ahead" on a sorely needed project, the airport in Prince Edward Island.
I want the parliamentary secretary to assure the minister- who is not the most popular figure in that part of Canada- that he will have my full and sustained support in bringing to Charlottetown a much needed airport with the most modern facilities that our province requires and needs. I will support the minister to the fullest extent of my eloquence and capacity as either a has-been politician or emeritus one, depending upon whether it is friend or enemy who describes me. I should like the parliamentary secretary to know that we appreciate his attention.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-CONSTRUCTION OF FACILITIES AT CHARLOTTETOWN-ALLEGED DELAY FOR ECONOMIC REASONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the views of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) when he describes his province of Prince Edward Island as one of the jewels of Canadian tourist life. I am sure-in fact that is the very reason why the Department of Transport decided to spend a relatively large amount of money on the Charlottetown airport-I am sure that everything in our power must be done to give better services to the visitors who go to Prince Edward Island as well, if not, in particular, Mr. Speaker, to the citizens of the island. I should like to thank the hon. member for his words of support for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). I agree with him that the needs of the people living near the airport must be taken into consideration and efforts made to
May 11, 1978

try to solve the sociological problems caused by having to move and the construction of a larger airport in the vicinity.

As the hon. member mentioned in his intervention, on November 8, 1977, the Minister of Transport announced that the federal government will completely redevelop the Charlottetown airport at a total cost of $21,531,500, to include a new terminal building and eventually a new 5,000 foot runway. I can assure the hon. member that this amount will not be diminished and that we will forgo the previous engagement we took last November. The Minister of Transport said at that time, and I quote:
This massive project indicates the government's longstanding commitment to improve transportation facilities in this province and throughout Atlantic Canada.
Adjournment Debate
The minister also paid tribute to the dynamic and highly successful Prince Edward Island tourism program since jet service began in 1969, which has resulted in a dramatic increase in air transportation. The Charlottetown airport redevelopment concept was developed in close consultation and co-operation with provincial and municipal authorities.
It is worth repeating that the carriers serving Charlottetown participated fully in the development of the master plan which identified a requirement for a new runway in future years. The first state of the new runway would be constructed to a length of 5,000 feet. As and when the demand developed, it would be extended to 7,000 feet. If at that time aviation technology has changed to the point where an even longer runway is required, operational requirements will be met.
